## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_How long can a robot act on a remembered scene after it loses sight of it?_

A person hidden behind a storage rack can keep moving while the robot's map still shows an empty aisle. Forgetting the person loses a constraint on motion; preserving the last position indefinitely turns old evidence into false certainty. The engineer must retain useful state through brief sensing gaps while limiting how long it can support a decision. That limit depends on the motion the sensors cannot observe, the error already present, and the clearance the task can tolerate. A stored estimate must therefore carry both its physical age and the conditions under which its uncertainty remains bounded. The permission path needs that information in time to refuse motion whose evidence has expired. Spatial memory connects sensing to the causal boundary by preserving what an observation supports without extending its authority beyond the physical margin.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Specify a spatial belief record that carries evidence age, uncertainty growth, and consumer query budgets
- Set belief expiry from bounded uncertainty growth and the task's physical tolerance
- Select a spatial representation for a clearance query from the query it answers, the memory reads it costs, and the storage it needs
- Trace how localization drift and loop closure move remembered map cells without renewing their evidence
- Design spatial updates that preserve evidence age and distinguish missing observations from verified free space
- Diagnose frozen transforms, phantom tracks, and unobservable drift that pass freshness and innovation checks

:::

## Spatial Belief Persistence and Representation {#sec-memory-preserving-belief}

A digital memory register can preserve a bit pattern indefinitely while the physical world it describes moves. As a warehouse mobile manipulator pivots away from the end of a storage rack, the rack uprights hide the cross aisle from the navigation camera, and whatever the vision backbone last detected there now survives only in memory. A person out of sight past the rack end can walk directly into the corridor that memory marks empty. Republishing that cached observation with a fresh software timestamp cannot restore the lost sensory evidence. Spatial memory must therefore carry the physical measurement epoch and an explicit uncertainty-growth law into every downstream motion-permission decision. The aisle stopping calculation so far covers a static obstacle at the declared clearance. A hidden approaching person changes that premise; the worked expiry calculation below shows why a separately qualified crossing control or an operating restriction is required.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Observation age and calibrated spatial covariances are generated in @sec-perception-observation-contract.
:::

A physical AI system cannot rely solely on instantaneous sensory observations or static KV-cache tensors. It requires a **belief**\index{Belief}, an estimate of physical state carried forward from historical sensory evidence, coupled explicitly to an expanding model of uncertainty.[^fn-mem-belief-state] Perception supplies a dated, calibrated observation (as established in @sec-perception-handoff). Spatial memory must determine how long that observation, combined with dynamic motion models, can continue to authorize physical action before epistemic uncertainty consumes the machine's remaining safety clearance.

[^fn-mem-belief-state]: **Belief state formulation**\index{State estimation!belief state}: In a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), a belief represents a probability distribution over latent states. A physical state interface additionally carries an error bound. Without the value, frame, evidence epoch, and applicable uncertainty model, a downstream optimizer cannot evaluate clearance during a sensor dropout.

As the second of the four proposal-side stages of Part III, between perception and intent, **spatial memory**\index{Spatial memory} carries geometric and physical state estimates forward across sensor dropouts, occlusions, and variable processing delays. It sits above the proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), so a remembered state can shape a proposal but cannot certify its own freshness; the permission path checks the age of the evidence against its own monotonic clock.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_sp.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Sense-Plan belief edge."}
*The Sense $\cap$ Plan belief interface: preserving spatial object state under line-of-sight occlusions.*
:::

A learned policy's context retains information according to an attention and storage budget. A person who disappears behind a pallet rack can be evicted from that context while still constraining the robot's motion, which makes an internal attention cache an unsuitable sole record of physical state. Spatial memory instead preserves the entity, its last observation, and the uncertainty that grows while it remains hidden.

Externalizing that state also separates the consumers' work. A policy retrieves a compact **spatial attention working set** around its candidate route from the host-resident scene map. An isolated permission controller instead consumes a bounded local safety snapshot, qualified for its clearance queries and available in its own memory. That snapshot preserves the source evidence epochs, uncertainty, coverage, and validity region; copying it does not make it fresh. The full map need not fit on the permission controller, and the controller must not wait for a host query to complete before deciding whether existing motion remains admissible.

Internal memory integrity alone cannot establish physical geometric validity. To prevent a machine from acting on stale data, memory systems must treat expiry as an explicit interface event. Each belief carries a deadline, its invalidation horizon (derived in @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion), at which its declared error bound reaches the task's physical margin. At that deadline the belief stops supporting motion, and the permission path refuses any proposal that still depends on it and selects a feasible fallback.

A belief that must declare its own expiry has to travel with more than its value, so the first handoff question is what a consumer needs to evaluate a stored value after its sensor loses sight of the object.

## The Spatial Memory Handoff and State Invariants {#sec-memory-handoff}

A position vector arriving over an inter-process bus cannot identify the entity, quantity, or units it describes. The same numbers could denote a workpiece center in meters, a joint angle in radians, or a contact force in newtons. A consumer needs those distinctions before applying a control law; a meters-to-millimeters mismatch alone changes the interpreted displacement by a thousandfold. The spatial belief record therefore begins with entity identity, physical quantity, and measurement units, rather than relying on conventions hidden in the producing model or transport wrapper.

Specifying the quantity and units remains incomplete without binding the value to a concrete reference frame. Identical spatial coordinates describe entirely different physical realities depending on the origin and orientation of the coordinate system. A Cartesian position $[0.142, -0.051, 0.812]\text{ m}$ designates a point suspended in free space when evaluated in the robot base frame\index{Base frame}, but represents a point several hundred millimeters inside a rigid fixture when interpreted in the tool flange frame\index{Tool flange frame}. Because kinematic links flex, joints move, and coordinate transforms update at varying rates, a belief record must carry an explicit frame identifier. Carrying the frame allows the receiving node to look up the corresponding spatial transformation tree and project the stored geometry into the local frame required by the actuator, preventing the controller from acting on geometric misalignments caused by moving kinematic chains.

Geometry and identity describe physical state at a single moment, but spatial memory must also capture the temporal anchor of that state. The record carries the evidence epoch $t_0$ of the physical interaction or optical exposure that last constrained the estimate at the causal boundary. In distributed machine architectures, intermediate nodes often republish data, execute Kalman filter prediction steps, or run forward kinematic propagations to maintain high-rate control streams; none of these computational steps adds physical evidence. The evidence epoch must therefore pass unchanged through every republish, filter, and prediction stage, so that consumers measure the age of the information against the physical world rather than against the scheduling frequency of the local computer.

Generating this anchored belief relies on **multi-sensor state estimation**\index{State estimation!contract boundary}\index{Sensor fusion!informational contract}. An estimator combines asynchronous observations with a motion model to infer the state between measurements [@kalman1960new]. Consumers need the resulting state, its justified error model, and the physical evidence that constrains each relevant component. They do not need to reproduce the estimator. A prediction step advances the estimate epoch while its evidence continues aging; a fresh measurement renews only the state dimensions it actually constrains. The covariance propagation mechanics are collected in @sec-appendix-control-covariance. Here the engineering obligation is to expose bounded growth through occlusion and withdraw claims whose assumptions no longer hold.

Knowing the evidence epoch $t_0$ establishes elapsed time $\Delta t = t - t_0$, but elapsed time alone cannot determine whether a belief is valid for a given action. Two estimates of identical age diverge at different rates depending on physical constraints. The rack end itself is bolted to the floor, so its remembered position can remain useful while the machine's localization bound and the fixed-rack premise hold, whereas a person hidden behind it can move at walking speed and close the narrow gap beside it before the next camera frame arrives.

The minimum record fields necessary for a consumer to evaluate a stored state can be derived directly from the requirement to bound current error. Let $E(\Delta t)$ represent the upper bound of the discrepancy between the stored value and true physical state after an elapsed time $\Delta t = t - t_0$. If an estimator establishes a state at time $t_0$ with an initial uncertainty bound\index{Uncertainty bound} $E_0$, and external disturbances or unmodeled velocities cause the true state to diverge at a maximum rate $r$, the upper bound on error at current time $t$ obeys the linear expansion\index{Error expansion} $E(\Delta t) = E_0 + r\,\Delta t$. At the rack end the stored claim is spatial, that no person stands near the machine; $E_0$ is then the machine's localization error, $r$ is the walking speed at which a person the rack hides can advance on the machine, and the tolerance is the depth of observed free space the machine does not need as clearance. @Sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion evaluates that law. Under the stochastic acceleration-noise model developed below, double integration produces cubic growth of position variance ($\propto t^3$). Omitting the initial bound or the dynamic growth terms leaves the consumer unable to compute $E(\Delta t)$, so an initial bound and an explicit expansion model are both structurally required fields of the record.

Expressing uncertainty through physical bounds and expansion rates distinguishes a physical AI belief from a probabilistic confidence score. An object detection network might output a class confidence of $0.94$, but that softmax score is not calibrated evidence (@sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities), and a downstream position controller cannot convert a unitless probability into a safe actuator displacement margin (i.e., how far the arm can physically move before risking a collision). A confidence score of $0.94$ provides no information about whether an obstacle boundary is uncertain by $2.0\text{ mm}$ or by $200\text{ mm}$, nor does it indicate how rapidly that boundary moves when occlusion occurs. A physical memory record must express its initial bound $E_0$ and expansion rate $r$ in concrete physical dimensions such as meters, radians, or newtons per second. Furthermore, these rates are valid only within a declared validity region, such as a maximum assumed acceleration or a verified contact friction coefficient. If physical operating conditions leave that region, the expansion rate no longer holds, and the belief record must be treated as invalid.

When the gripper finger approaches the latch-release slot, the consumer compares the belief's current error with the slot clearance. It converts the evidence epoch into its own clock, includes the clock-conversion bound, and evaluates the declared growth law at the time the state will be used. This is a continuing obligation during execution, not a one-time path-generation check. A new proposal whose evidence fails the check is refused without automatically revoking a still-valid active command. If the active motion itself depends on expiring evidence, the controller must begin a feasible fallback early enough that the response remains within the available clearance. The belief's expiry is a limit on supported motion, not a promise that an instantaneous stop is possible at that instant.

::: {#dfn-memory-spatial-belief-contract .callout-definition title="Spatial belief record"}

***Spatial belief record***\index{Spatial belief record!definition}\index{Belief record!definition} is the seventh record in the record chain. It binds identified physical quantities and map regions to a reference frame, hardware evidence epochs, estimate epochs, clock-conversion bounds, uncertainty-growth laws, operating validity regions, task expiries, provenance, and lifecycle status. Each consumer also receives a query-work limit appropriate to its deadline. The record makes these claims checkable; qualification must establish that they hold.

1.  **Significance**: Consumers can distinguish a useful prediction from fresh evidence and determine when its error exhausts the task clearance. The worked local collision interface allocates at most $2\ \mu\text{s}$ per query; that allocation is derived from its workload rather than imposed on every scene representation.
2.  **Distinction**: A belief record couples physical units and evidence age to an error-growth model. A classification score, map publication time, or transform value alone cannot supply that contract.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Waiting for an upstream publisher to announce expiry. If its thread hangs or its messages stop, the consumer must still age the evidence and enforce its own deadline.

:::

Evaluating the spatial belief record depends on calculating the elapsed time $\Delta t = t_{\text{now}} - t_0$ against physical reality. If the consumer cannot verify the exact physical instant when energy transduction occurred, the calculated error bound $E(\Delta t)$ becomes an unanchored fiction, mistaking software compute cycles for physical evidence. The estimate epoch and clock conversion named in the definition exist to protect that anchor, while provenance and lifecycle status, the record's remaining fields, are developed with the schema in @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema.

## State Epochs and Temporal Anchoring {#sec-memory-state-epoch}

A bounding box or 3D Gaussian pose emitted by a neural object detector describes where an entity was when photons struck the camera CMOS sensor, not where it is when the inference tensor arrives in memory. Every spatial claim refers to a specific physical instant, its **epoch**\index{Epoch}, and any state crossing a physical AI pipeline carries three distinct epochs before an actuator can fire. The **acquisition epoch**\index{Epoch!acquisition} ($t_0$) is the capture epoch of the observation contract (@sec-perception-observation-contract)—the observation's physical time reference, such as the exposure midpoint for the camera or the instant a hardware register latches an encoder count—which spatial memory anchors as its evidence epoch. Spatial memory adds the two epochs that follow it. The **estimate epoch**\index{Epoch!estimate} ($t_{\text{est}}$) marks the physical instant that the estimated state describes. A predictor can advance that instant beyond the last observation without obtaining new evidence; the time at which computation finishes is a separate scheduling fact. The **publication epoch**\index{Epoch!publication} ($t_{\text{pub}}$) marks the instant the serialized state record was committed to the transport bus or shared-memory ring buffer for dispatch to downstream consumers.

Collapsing these three timestamps into one receipt or transmission timestamp destroys the physical anchor. This **publish-time stamping anti-pattern**\index{Publish-time stamping anti-pattern!definition} occurs when a wrapper stamps its output with the current software clock after exposure, transport, inference, and postprocessing have already elapsed. The receiver then sees a recent message containing old evidence. The age-as-displacement relation established in @sec-perception-photons-to-claims still applies throughout that pipeline. Publication time helps diagnose scheduling delay, but only acquisition time lets a motion consumer account for the world's change since the measurement.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Synchronized hardware timestamping across fieldbuses is established in @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses.
:::

Even when a system records true acquisition epochs, physical AI architectures rely on distributed processing nodes whose local oscillator clocks drift independently. The deployed clock-conversion protocol must establish an error bound under its stated load and fault conditions; a bus interface alone supplies no such guarantee. That temporal uncertainty becomes spatial uncertainty at the relative speed of whatever the record describes.[^fn-hw-ptp-canfd] The observation record of @sec-perception-observation-contract already carries this bound as its clock-conversion error, and a belief built from that observation keeps it. Every consumer adds the bound to the evidence age before judging freshness, and the error budget allocates the distance that bound covers at the record's relative speed alongside sensor resolution and structural deflection. In safety enforcement, downstream Control Barrier Functions treat this clock-synchronization uncertainty $\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$ as an irreducible temporal margin, inflating the required spatial barrier clearance by $d_{\text{sync}} = v_{\text{rel}} \epsilon_{\text{sync}}$ before granting motor torque authorization.

[^fn-hw-ptp-canfd]: **Fieldbus clock synchronization jitter**\index{Fieldbus!synchronization jitter}: CAN-FD bit-phase synchronization aligns bit sampling within a frame; it does not synchronize the distributed clocks that date physical observations. A shared evidence-time basis requires a specified clock-conversion protocol and a qualified bound on its offset and drift. PTP and EtherCAT Distributed Clocks provide synchronization mechanisms, but their names alone do not establish the deployed error bound. The allowed temporal error follows from the task's spatial allocation and relative velocity ($e_{\text{sync}} = v_{\text{rel}} \delta t$).

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-epoch-alignment
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ILLUSTRATIVE SAMPLING EPOCHS FOR FUSION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-state-epoch (three sensors latch at different epochs).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that fusing two observations requires projecting one across
# │          the gap between their acquisition epochs.
# │ Show:    tactile 12 ms, camera 18.5 ms, encoders 21 ms; camera-to-encoder
# │          gap 2.5 ms.
# │ How:     Illustrative epochs in one cycle; the gap is |t3 - t2|.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

class MemoryEpochAlignment:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    t1 = 12.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (tactile array latches force)
    t2 = 18.5 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (camera exposure midpoint)
    t3 = 21.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (encoders sample angles)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    gap = abs(t3 - t2).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t1 < t2 < t3, "The illustrative epochs must be in sampling order.")
    check(abs(gap.magnitude - 2.5) < 1e-9, "Camera-to-encoder gap is 2.5 ms.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    t1_str = fmt_latency(t1, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t2_str = fmt_latency(t2, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t3_str = fmt_latency(t3, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    gap_str = fmt_latency(gap, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Physical systems often combine asynchronously acquired signals, even though hardware triggers can align selected sensors. In an illustrative asynchronous cycle, a tactile array might latch normal force readings at $t_1 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t1_str`, an optical tracking camera might have its exposure midpoint at $t_2 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t2_str`, and joint optical encoders might sample angular positions at $t_3 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t3_str`. These observations occur at different epochs and cannot be combined through direct tensor concatenation or algebraic operations. In multimodal foundation models and vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, visual tokens, proprioceptive vectors, and tactile embeddings are frequently packed into a single attention sequence under the implicit assumption that all tokens capture a simultaneous physical snapshot. Nothing in that packing records that the hand position came from $t_2$ and the joint reading from $t_3$, so whatever the model infers from their combination carries no bound on the error the mismatch introduces. Fusing a camera observation at $t_2$ with an encoder observation at $t_3$ requires the consumer to project one state across the temporal gap $\Delta t = |t_3 - t_2| =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.gap_str` using explicit kinematic models and bounded velocities (for example, propagating the historical camera observation along the joint velocity vector to reconcile it with the instantaneous encoder reading). Without the true acquisition epoch for each individual signal, the alignment calculation cannot determine the sign or magnitude of $\Delta t$, compounding geometric errors across every inference cycle.

With these epochs and the clock-synchronization bound carried in the record of @sec-memory-handoff, the consumer computes the elapsed duration between the evidence epoch and the execution deadline, evaluates the worst-case expansion of the error bound, and determines whether the state remains within task tolerances. Handing over a state without its acquisition epoch leaves the consumer blind to transport delays and scheduling jitter, turning deterministic control into open-loop guesswork. Because physical geometry also changes as bodies move through space, spatial transforms between reference frames are subject to the same temporal decay, carrying their own distinct evidence epochs.

## Coordinate Transform Expiry and Calibration Drift {#sec-memory-reference-frames}

A coordinate frame binds a spatial representation, but in an active physical machine the frame itself moves. In embodied architectures, sensors, chassis links, and end-effectors are related through a directed acyclic transform graph. What the static graph does not show is how an edge goes stale. Each edge of the tree in @fig-09-robot-transform-tree stores a rigid-body pose parameterized by joint angles [@lynch2017modern; @craig2005introduction], and that pose describes the machine only at the epoch when its physical geometry was transduced. When an onboard computer chains transforms measured at different times—due to neural inference latency, transport delay, asynchronous sensor sampling, or dropped frames—the mathematical product is a hybrid pose that the physical machine never occupied (@sec-appendix-control-spatial defines coordinate mapping and transform-chain composition).

A transform also spans several machine words (six or seven floating-point numbers for translations and rotation quaternions), so a high-rate control reader racing an asynchronous vision writer can observe an old rotation paired with a new translation. The lock-free seqlock mailbox established in @sec-nervous-cadences closes this concurrency race without blocking hard real-time control threads: each reader makes one bounded attempt per tick and never waits; a torn read is discarded, and the last validated transform ages in its place.

::: {#fig-09-robot-transform-tree fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Manipulator kinematic frame tree and temporal dynamics**: Articulated manipulator geometry (a) and corresponding directed acyclic coordinate transform tree in ROS \\texttt{tf2} (b). Each directed edge stores a homogeneous transformation matrix parameterized by joint state. Composing transforms across disparate acquisition epochs injects lever-arm positioning error $e_{\\text{tool}} \\approx \\ell\\,\\Delta\\theta$, while an uncompensated asynchronous edge references stale coordinates (adapted from Craig 2005 and Foote 2013 [@craig2005introduction; @foote2013tf])." fig-alt="Manipulator Kinematic Frame Tree and Temporal Lever-Arm Dynamics. (a) Physical geometry of an articulated manipulator with base link, joint linkages, wrist camera, and tool center point (tool0), indicating lever arm ℓ and angular deflection error e_tool ≈ ℓ · Δθ. (b) Spatial transformation tree (DAG) connecting world reference, base link, kinematic chain link1 through link6, wrist frame, wrist camera, tool0 TCP, and target object, highlighting an asynchronous stale transform edge. (Adapted from Craig 2005 and Foote 2013)."}
![](images/svg/fig09_canonical_robot_frame_tree.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In @fig-09-robot-transform-tree, panel (a) illustrates the physical geometry of an articulated serial manipulator carrying an eye-in-hand wrist camera and an end-effector tool center point (`tool0`). Mechanical links (`link1` through `link6`) are connected by revolute joints whose optical encoders continuously sample joint angles $\theta_i(t)$. The tool tip extends beyond the wrist joint by an effective lever arm $\ell$. When the wrist turns at angular rate $\omega$, any temporal latency $\Delta t$ in the wrist coordinate frame introduces an angular lag $\Delta\theta = \omega\,\Delta t$, sweeping the tool tip across an unmodeled circular arc $e_{\text{tool}} \approx \ell\,\Delta\theta$.

Panel (b) depicts the corresponding coordinate transform tree maintained as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in robot middleware such as ROS `tf2` [@foote2013tf]. Each directed edge represents a $4 \times 4$ homogeneous transformation matrix $\mathbf{T}_{A \leftarrow B}$ mapping points from child frame $B$ into parent frame $A$. Because internal joint encoders publish at high cadences (typically $500\text{--}1{,}000\text{ Hz}$) over deterministic fieldbuses while external visual perception pipelines publish target poses (`target_object`) at camera framerates ($30\text{--}60\text{ Hz}$) over asynchronous network transports, the transform tree inevitably buffers edges with disparate timestamps. The library itself refuses to mix them. A `tf2` lookup for a chain at time $t$ resolves every edge at that same $t$, interpolating each edge between its buffered samples, and it raises an extrapolation error when $t$ lies beyond an edge's latest sample; a request for "the latest" transform returns the chain at the latest time common to all its edges, which is again a single consistent epoch [@foote2013tf]. Hybrid poses come from application code that bypasses those semantics. A node that caches an edge, composes an object pose carried in a detection message with a separate lookup of the arm at "now," or republishes an old edge under a new stamp multiplies the current forward kinematics $\mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{wrist}}(t)$ with a stale vision edge $\mathbf{T}_{\text{wrist} \leftarrow \text{object}}(t - \Delta t)$. That composition is the **chimeric kinematic product anti-pattern**\index{Chimeric kinematic product anti-pattern!definition}: an unphysical hybrid pose that the robot never occupied.

The same-time rule leaves the application one decision, what to do when the requested time lies beyond the newest sample. A lookup can fail immediately, or a noncritical caller can wait subject to a timeout. The permission path requires bounded, nonblocking lookup and explicit rejection on failure. An application that instead predicts the transform must carry a validated growth bound; naive extrapolation during a communication stall otherwise accumulates lever-arm error $e_{\text{rot}} \approx \ell\,\omega\,\Delta t$.

The cost of an expired transform is direct spatial displacement (@fig-frame-staleness-error). Applying the age-as-displacement relation of @sec-perception-photons-to-claims to kinematics, uncompensated latency translates directly into geometric positioning error through the lever arm of the linkages. For the rigorous cross-product derivation of this kinematic error propagation, see @sec-appendix-control-spatial.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-latch-transform-staleness
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STALE SLOT-TO-FINGER TRANSFORM AT THE LATCH SLOT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-reference-frames (lever-arm staleness example); owns
# │          the latch-slot constants that @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion
# │          (LatchSlotBelief) reads.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that one missed wrist-camera frame on the slot-to-finger
# │          edge can spend more than the latch-release slot's tolerance, most
# │          of it through the lever arm.
# │ Show:    the frame period, the lateral drift at the finger's drift bound,
# │          the lever-arm arc, and their sum with E0 against the slot.
# │ How:     e_tool ~ E0 + v_drift dt + l omega dt, dt one wrist-camera frame.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LatchTransformStaleness:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    frame_rate = RM.wrist_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet (wrist camera)
    e0 = 0.1 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (finger-to-slot error at the wrist capture)
    v_drift = 12.0 * ureg.millimeter / ureg.second  # category: illustrative (unobserved lateral velocity error bound)
    e_max = 1.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (latch-release slot tolerance)
    lever = 0.15 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (wrist-to-fingertip lever arm)
    omega = 0.30 * ureg.radian / ureg.second  # category: illustrative (wrist rate while aligning the finger)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    dt = (1 / frame_rate).to(millisecond)
    e_trans = (v_drift * dt).to(ureg.millimeter)
    e_rot = (lever * omega * dt / ureg.radian).to(ureg.millimeter)
    e_tool = (e0 + e_trans + e_rot).to(ureg.millimeter)
    ratio = (e_tool / e_max).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dt.magnitude - 16.667) < 1e-3, f"Wrist-camera frame period should be 16.7 ms, got {dt}.")
    check(abs(e_trans.magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-6, f"Lateral drift over one frame should be 0.20 mm, got {e_trans}.")
    check(abs(e_rot.magnitude - 0.75) < 1e-6, f"Lever-arm arc should be 0.75 mm, got {e_rot}.")
    check(e_rot > e_trans, "The lever arm must contribute more than the lateral drift.")
    check(e_tool > e_max, "One missed frame must exceed the slot tolerance.")
    check(abs(e_tool.magnitude - 1.05) < 1e-6, f"Total finger error should be 1.05 mm, got {e_tool}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    dt_str = fmt_latency(dt, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    e0_str = fmt_length(e0, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    v_drift_str = fmt_velocity(v_drift, unit=ureg.millimeter / ureg.second, precision=0)
    lever_str = fmt_length(lever, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    omega_str = fmt_angular_velocity(omega, precision=2)
    e_trans_str = fmt_length(e_trans, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_rot_str = fmt_length(e_rot, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_tool_str = fmt_length(e_tool, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    e_max_str = fmt_length(e_max, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    ratio_pct_str = fmt_percent(ratio - 1, precision=0, style="prose")
```

How little staleness it takes to spend a task's tolerance shows at the latch-release slot, while the wrist camera can still see it. Each wrist-camera frame, one every `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.dt_str`, renews the slot's pose in the camera frame and with it the slot-to-finger edge the controller aligns on, and the finger must stay within the slot tolerance $E_{\max}$ of `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_max_str`. To isolate the effect of one frame period, suppose the supporting observation is available at its capture epoch, with ingestion delay idealized as zero, and the edge then ages by one frame period. A deployed edge is already older when ingestion completes; its consumer must qualify and charge the full capture-to-use age, including processing, transport, and any additional missed frames. Starting from an initial error of `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e0_str`, the finger's lateral offset drifts at most $e_{\text{trans}} = v_{\text{drift}}\,\Delta t$ under an illustrative `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.v_drift_str` bound on its unobserved lateral velocity, validated for the arm's operating region, or `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_trans_str`. With the fingertip an illustrative $\ell$ = `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.lever_str` beyond the wrist and the wrist turning at an illustrative $\omega$ = `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.omega_str` as it aligns the finger, the lever arm adds $e_{\text{rot}} \approx \ell\,\omega\,\Delta t$, or `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_rot_str`. The joint encoders measure that turn, but an application that composes the cached slot edge, dated to the previous frame, with the current wrist pose obtains a hybrid pose, a finger position the arm never held. Only chaining the slot against the wrist pose of its own capture epoch, which a same-time lookup does, or expiring the edge, removes that arc. Left in the chain, the stale edge misplaces the finger by `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_tool_str`, `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.ratio_pct_str` more than the slot allows, and more of that error comes from the lever arm than from the drift. Because the hand-composed product evaluates without error, nothing flags the stale pose, and the controller keeps aligning the finger on a slot position that is off by more than the clearance, which on an unfavorable approach puts the finger against the strike plate beside the slot.

::: {#fig-frame-staleness-error fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Transform staleness and lever-arm error at the latch-release slot**: Illustrative finger error over one frame period, with zero ingestion delay assumed to isolate this contribution. A deployed calculation must use full capture-to-use age. The slot-to-finger edge ages by duration $\\Delta t$. Lateral drift at the velocity bound $v_{\\text{drift}}$ moves the finger by $e_{\\text{trans}} = v_{\\text{drift}}\\,\\Delta t$, while the wrist turning at $\\omega$ swings the fingertip, a lever arm $\\ell$ beyond it, by $e_{\\text{rot}} \\approx \\ell\\,\\omega\\,\\Delta t$. Composing the stale edge with the current wrist pose adds both to the initial error $E_0$, so the finger error $e_{\\text{tool}} \\approx E_0 + e_{\\text{trans}} + \\ell\\,\\Delta\\theta$ exceeds the slot tolerance $E_{\\max}$." fig-alt="Transform staleness at the latch-release slot. A dashed ghost arm shows the wrist and finger as dated by the stale edge at t0, with a dashed circle marking the slot tolerance E_max around the finger. The current arm at t0 + Δt shows the wrist shifted laterally by e_trans = v_drift Δt and the link of length ℓ turned by Δθ = ω Δt, which swings the finger by e_rot ≈ ℓ Δθ. A red vector from the stale finger position to the current finger, labeled e_tool ≈ E_0 + e_trans + ℓ Δθ, ends well outside the E_max circle."}
![](images/svg/fig09_frame_staleness_error.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The red vector in @fig-frame-staleness-error crosses the tolerance boundary even though every matrix multiplication remains valid. The worked calculation locates the dominant error in the wrist's lever arm, so increasing timestamp precision alone would not repair the chain. The consumer must compose compatible epochs or reject the expired edge.

::: {#psp-memory-leverage-of-staleness .callout-perspective title="The leverage of staleness"}
*A transform's admissible age is set at the point it serves, not at the joint it measures. The tool point drifts at roughly $v + \ell\omega$, so the longer the lever arm, the sooner an edge expires, and an edge still fresh enough to locate the wrist can be too old to locate the tool center point.*
:::

### Localization drift and map frames that jump {#sec-memory-localization-slam}

The arm's transforms come from encoders that measure every joint. The base has no such anchor. Every map-anchored belief in this chapter, and every row of the stopping budget, inherits the localization bound $\delta_{\text{loc}}$, the claim that the machine knows where it stands in its map to within that distance. That claim is produced by two estimators with opposite failure modes, and a memory that stores map cells has to know which one it is leaning on.

**Odometry**\index{Odometry} integrates incremental motion from wheel encoders, the inertial unit, or scan-to-scan lidar matching. It is smooth and fast, but it observes only increments, never absolute position, so the small error in each increment accumulates without bound; position is the unobservable direction of @sec-memory-state-estimation-bounds, here along the aisle. **Map-based localization**\index{Localization!map-based} matches the current scan against a stored map and bounds that error, at the cost of arriving as discrete corrections. **Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)**\index{SLAM} builds the map while localizing against it. Modern SLAM stores the trajectory as a pose graph, a factor graph whose nodes are past poses and whose factors are odometry and scan-match constraints; when the machine recognizes a place it has visited before, a **loop closure**\index{Loop closure} adds a constraint between the two visits, and re-solving the graph moves past poses to spread the accumulated drift back along the trajectory [@thrun2005probabilistic; @cadena2016past; @dellaert2017factor; @hess2016real]. The filter mechanics that fuse odometry with a correction are those of @sec-perception-discrete-state-estimation; what matters here is what each estimator does to the age and position of stored evidence.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-odometry-drift
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ODOMETRY DRIFT AGAINST THE LOCALIZATION BOUND
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-localization-slam (where delta_loc comes from).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that odometry alone cannot hold the budget's localization
# │          bound over one aisle, so delta_loc is a premise about how often
# │          map corrections arrive.
# │ Show:    distance and time at the aisle speed before relative drift alone
# │          spends delta_loc; drift accumulated over one aisle length.
# │ How:     d = delta_loc / eps_drift; t = d / v_aisle; e_aisle = eps * L.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class OdometryDrift:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative (budget localization bound)
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen (aisle speed)
    aisle_length = AISLE.aisle_length  # category: illustrative (aisle length)
    eps_drift = 0.01  # category: illustrative; NEEDS SOURCE (odometry error per meter traveled on the site floor, from a ground-truth drive test)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_budget = (delta_loc / eps_drift).to(ureg.meter)
    t_budget = (d_budget / v_aisle).to(ureg.second)
    e_aisle = (eps_drift * aisle_length).to(ureg.millimeter)
    aisle_ratio = (e_aisle / delta_loc).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(d_budget.magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"Odometry distance budget should be 5 m, got {d_budget}.")
    check(d_budget < aisle_length, "Odometry alone must not hold delta_loc over one aisle.")
    check(abs(aisle_ratio - 6.0) < 1e-9, f"Drift over one aisle should be 6x delta_loc, got {aisle_ratio}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    eps_pct_str = fmt_percent(eps_drift, precision=0, style="prose")
    d_budget_str = fmt_length(d_budget, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    t_budget_str = fmt_latency(t_budget, unit=ureg.second, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    aisle_length_str = fmt_length(aisle_length, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    e_aisle_str = fmt_length(e_aisle, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    aisle_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(aisle_ratio, precision=0)
```

A number shows why $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ is a premise about corrections rather than a property of the base. Suppose, as an illustrative value that a site drive test must replace, that the base's odometry drifts by `{python} OdometryDrift.eps_pct_str` of the distance it travels. The `{python} OdometryDrift.delta_loc_str` bound is then spent after `{python} OdometryDrift.d_budget_str` of travel, `{python} OdometryDrift.t_budget_str` at the `{python} OdometryDrift.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, and one `{python} OdometryDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle on odometry alone accumulates `{python} OdometryDrift.e_aisle_str`, `{python} OdometryDrift.aisle_ratio_mult_str` the bound. The budget's localization row therefore holds only while map corrections arrive more often than the drift budget runs out. The measurement that supplies the drift rate is a ground-truth drive: the base traverses the site's aisles past surveyed markers, and the recorded odometry error per meter, taken at a stated percentile over the floor conditions the site permits, replaces the illustrative value.

Loop closure raises a problem that no single-epoch record anticipates. A map cell stored in the map frame keeps its evidence epoch, because the photons that observed it are exactly as old as they were, yet its position changes when the graph re-solves the pose it hangs from. The cell's evidence is not renewed, and its location is suddenly different. A snapshot copied before the closure therefore places that cell wrong by up to the size of the correction, while every timestamp in it still passes an age check. A map belief must carry the revision of the pose graph that placed it alongside its cell epochs, and a closure that moves the supporting poses must either re-anchor the dependent snapshots or expire them.

The robotics convention for mobile bases, ROS REP 105, separates the two estimators into frames so that consumers can choose the property they need [@meeussen2010rep105]. The `odom` frame carries odometry: the base's pose in it is continuous, never jumping, but drifts without bound. The `map` frame carries localization: the pose in it does not drift significantly, but it can change in discrete jumps whenever a correction or closure arrives. The localizer publishes the `map`-to-`odom` transform, so a correction moves that one edge and leaves the chain from `odom` to `base_link` smooth. The permission controller's local snapshot belongs in the continuous frame. Over the few seconds a snapshot lives, drift in `odom` accumulates slowly and can be charged against $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ from the distance traveled since the snapshot was built, whereas a snapshot held in `map` would see its hull teleport by the size of every correction. Goals, the host map, and snapshot construction stay in `map`; after a correction the host rebuilds the snapshot rather than letting the controller absorb the jump. The `map`-to-`odom` edge is itself a transform with an evidence epoch, and the rules of this section apply to it like any other edge.

A stale transform displaces both the tool estimate and any observations mapped through it. The surrounding world ages too, but it has no joint encoders to report its motion. Memory must therefore record which surfaces and empty regions the sensors actually verified, as well as the frames in which those observations hold.

## Certified Spatial Assertions in Scene Memory {#sec-memory-scene-attention-buffers}

After the robot sweeps its range sensor down an aisle, memory must distinguish space it saw occupied, space it saw empty, and space it never saw. Only observed empty space can support a clearance claim, and only while that evidence remains valid. A map that merges unknown space with free space defeats the evidence-age checks even if every stored timestamp is correct.

The representation must also serve consumers with different needs. A learned policy needs object identity and local geometry to propose a route or grasp. The permission path needs bounded geometric queries whose evidence can be checked before its deadline. Metric maps supply distances and occupancy, scene graphs organize those quantities into objects and places, and episodic memory preserves the interaction history needed to interpret them. These layers share evidence without giving a semantic label or remembered event authority to certify clearance.

### Volumetric metric maps and distance fields {#sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps}

The aisle clearance query asks the map for one quantity, the distance from a body hull to the nearest place that is occupied, unobserved, or no longer vouched for. A rendering query asks for something else, what a camera at a given pose would see. A representation earns a place on the permission path by answering the first question, within the time the permission tick allows, from storage the permission controller actually has. We therefore allocate the query workload first, count what each representation must read to answer it, and only then size the storage.

#### Collision query latency deadlines for reactive safety filters {.unnumbered}

The worked design allocates spatial collision checking within a $1\text{ kHz}$ permission loop ($T_{\text{tick}} = 1{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$). The required query returns conservative clearance at each body collision hull; where the selected filter needs a gradient, that work belongs in the same measured query. For the illustrative $N_{\text{hulls}} = 20\text{--}50$ evaluation spheres, the total work is:
$$T_{\text{query\_total}} = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\text{hulls}}} t_{\text{query}}(\mathbf{x}_k) \le T_{\text{reflex\_budget}}$$ {#eq-mem-query-latency-budget}
To bound the total collision workload in @eq-mem-query-latency-budget, the worked $N_{\text{hulls}} = 50$ case reserves $T_{\text{reflex\_budget}} = 100\ \mu\text{s}$ for local collision checking, leaving 90 percent of the tick for the other permission and communication work. This is an allocation to be tested on the deployed controller; full-map updates and trajectory optimization run outside this tick. Dividing the allocation among the hulls gives:
$$t_{\text{query}} \le \frac{T_{\text{reflex\_budget}}}{N_{\text{hulls}}} \approx \frac{100\ \mu\text{s}}{50} = 2.0\ \mu\text{s}$$

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-representation-query
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLEARANCE QUERY COST AND LOCAL SNAPSHOT STORAGE BY REPRESENTATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps (query semantics, read budget,
# │          snapshot sizing), @tbl-09-representation-queries,
# │          @fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto.
# │
# │ Goal:    Replace stipulated latencies with counts a reader can recompute:
# │          memory reads per sphere-hull clearance query, and the bytes a
# │          local snapshot of the stopping corridor needs.
# │ Show:    the per-query read budget on the permission MCU; reads for a
# │          dense occupancy scan, a worst-case octree scan, and an ESDF
# │          lookup at 2, 5, and 10 cm; snapshot bytes against MCU SRAM.
# │ How:     reads budget = t_query x SRAM bandwidth / cell bytes;
# │          occupancy scan = (4/3) pi ((r_hull + delta_margin) / r)^3 cells;
# │          octree = scan x ceil(log2(L_map / r)) dependent reads;
# │          ESDF = 8 reads (one trilinear lookup); snapshot = V_slab / r^3 x
# │          cell bytes; quantization = (sqrt 3 / 2) r.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty, fmt_qty_int

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

def _representation_rows(pitches_cm, reach, l_map, v_slab, s_esdf, s_occ, n_trilinear):
    rows = {}
    for cm in pitches_cm:
        r = cm * ureg.centimeter
        scan = 4 / 3 * math.pi * (reach / r).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude ** 3
        depth = math.ceil(math.log2((l_map / r).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude))
        cells = (v_slab / r**3).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
        rows[cm] = dict(
            occ_reads=scan,
            depth=depth,
            oct_reads=scan * depth,
            esdf_reads=n_trilinear,
            esdf_bytes=(cells * s_esdf).to(ureg.kilobyte),
            occ_bytes=(cells * s_occ).to(ureg.kilobyte),
            quant=(math.sqrt(3) / 2 * r).to(ureg.millimeter),
        )
    return rows

class RepresentationQuery:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    t_reflex = 100 * microsecond  # category: chosen (collision-check allocation within the 1 kHz tick)
    n_hulls = 50  # category: illustrative (sphere hulls covering the machine)
    r_hull = 0.25 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (sphere-hull radius)
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen (protective clearance)
    sram_bw = RM.permission_mcu.memory.sram_bandwidth  # category: datasheet (permission MCU SRAM, reference class)
    sram_cap = RM.permission_mcu.memory.sram_capacity  # category: datasheet (permission MCU SRAM, reference class)
    s_esdf = 8 * ureg.byte  # category: illustrative (4 B distance, 2 B weight, 2 B evidence epoch)
    s_occ = 4 * ureg.byte  # category: illustrative (2 B log-odds, 2 B evidence epoch)
    l_map = 10.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (host-map edge, the 10 m workcell below)
    aisle_width = AISLE.aisle_width  # category: illustrative (aisle width)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (clear distance ahead)
    h_slab = 2.0 * ureg.meter  # category: chosen (snapshot height covering the arm's reach)
    pitches_cm = (2, 5, 10)  # category: chosen (voxel pitches compared)
    n_trilinear = 8  # category: derived (corner cells of one trilinear interpolation)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_query = (t_reflex / n_hulls).to(microsecond)
    reads_budget = (t_query * sram_bw / s_esdf).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    reach = (r_hull + delta_margin).to(ureg.meter)
    v_slab = (aisle_width * d_clear * h_slab).to(ureg.meter**3)
    rows = _representation_rows(pitches_cm, reach, l_map, v_slab, s_esdf, s_occ, n_trilinear)
    r2, r5, r10 = rows[2], rows[5], rows[10]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_query.magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Per-query allocation should be 2 us, got {t_query}.")
    check(abs(reads_budget - 800) < 1e-6, f"Read budget should be 800 cells, got {reads_budget}.")
    check(r5["occ_reads"] > reads_budget > r10["occ_reads"], "An occupancy scan must fit only at the coarsest pitch.")
    check(r10["oct_reads"] > reads_budget, "A worst-case octree scan must miss the budget at every pitch.")
    check(n_trilinear < reads_budget, "An ESDF lookup must fit at every pitch.")
    check(r5["esdf_bytes"] < sram_cap < r2["esdf_bytes"], "The 5 cm snapshot must fit SRAM and the 2 cm one must not.")
    check(r10["quant"] > delta_margin / 2, "At 10 cm, quantization alone must exceed half the protective clearance.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_query_str = fmt_latency(t_query, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    sram_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(sram_bw, precision=1)
    sram_cap_str = fmt_memory(sram_cap, unit=ureg.megabyte, precision=2)
    reads_budget_str = fmt_int(reads_budget)
    r_hull_str = fmt_length(r_hull, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    reach_str = fmt_length(reach, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    v_slab_str = fmt_qty(v_slab, ureg.meter**3, precision=2)
    h_slab_str = fmt_length(h_slab, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    occ2_str, occ5_str, occ10_str = (fmt_int(r["occ_reads"]) for r in (r2, r5, r10))
    oct2_str, oct5_str, oct10_str = (fmt_int(r["oct_reads"]) for r in (r2, r5, r10))
    depth5_str = fmt_int(r5["depth"])
    esdf_reads_str = fmt_int(n_trilinear)
    esdf2_bytes_str = fmt_memory(r2["esdf_bytes"], unit=ureg.megabyte, precision=2)
    esdf5_bytes_str = fmt_qty_int(r5["esdf_bytes"], ureg.kilobyte)
    esdf10_bytes_str = fmt_memory(r10["esdf_bytes"], unit=ureg.kilobyte, precision=1)
    quant5_str = fmt_qty_int(r5["quant"], ureg.millimeter)
    quant10_str = fmt_qty_int(r10["quant"], ureg.millimeter)
```

A time allocation becomes a design constraint once it is expressed in the unit the hardware spends, memory reads. The permission controller streams its local SRAM at `{python} RepresentationQuery.sram_bw_str`, so the `{python} RepresentationQuery.t_query_str` allocation covers at most `{python} RepresentationQuery.reads_budget_str` reads of an 8-byte cell per hull query, before any arithmetic, cache effect, or contention; qualification on the deployed controller must still measure the real bound (@sec-placement). Against that ceiling, the representations differ less in speed than in which question one read answers (@tbl-09-representation-queries). An **occupancy grid**\index{Occupancy grid} stores, per cell, whether that cell is occupied [@elfes1989using; @moravec1985high]; certifying that a sphere hull of radius `{python} RepresentationQuery.r_hull_str` keeps its protective clearance means reading every cell within `{python} RepresentationQuery.reach_str` of its center, $\frac{4}{3}\pi\left((r_{\text{hull}}+\delta_{\text{margin}})/r\right)^3$ cells at pitch $r$. A hierarchical **octree** such as OctoMap [@hornung2013octomap] answers the same point query after descending the tree, one dependent read per level, so near surfaces, where pruning cannot merge cells, the scan costs its cell count times the tree depth. A **truncated signed distance field (TSDF)**\index{Truncated signed distance field} stores the distance to the nearest surface along the sensor ray, clamped at a truncation distance of a few voxels [@curless1996volumetric]; one read answers only whether a surface lies within that truncation, so "farther than the truncation" never certifies a clearance larger than it. A **Euclidean signed distance field (ESDF)**\index{Euclidean signed distance field} stores the straight-line distance to the nearest obstacle [@oleynikova2017voxblox; @millane2024nvblox], so one interpolated lookup, `{python} RepresentationQuery.esdf_reads_str` corner reads, certifies clearance for an entire sphere: the hull passes when the distance at its center exceeds $r_{\text{hull}} + \delta_{\text{margin}}$ plus the geometric error. Rendering representations answer the second question. A 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) scene fits anisotropic Gaussians to a photometric loss [@kerbl20233d], and a neural radiance field integrates learned density along camera rays; neither stores a conservative distance, and collision checking on splats requires an added assumption that the fitted ellipsoids enclose the physical surface [@chen2025splatnav]. Their parameterizations are collected in @sec-appendix-ml-3dgs, and the occupancy and TSDF update equations in @sec-appendix-ml-voxels.

| Representation         | Query one lookup answers                      |                  Reads per hull query at 5 cm | Can certify the hull's clearance?                        |
|:-----------------------|:----------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| Dense occupancy grid   | Is this cell occupied?                        |       `{python} RepresentationQuery.occ5_str` | Yes, by scanning every cell within reach                 |
| Octree occupancy       | Is this cell occupied? (after a tree descent) |       `{python} RepresentationQuery.oct5_str` | Yes, by the same scan, one descent per cell              |
| TSDF                   | Is a surface within the truncation distance?  |                                             1 | Only up to the truncation distance                       |
| ESDF                   | How far is the nearest obstacle?              | `{python} RepresentationQuery.esdf_reads_str` | Yes, with unknown cells treated as obstacles             |
| 3DGS or radiance field | What would a camera at this pose see?         |                                             — | No; requires a separately qualified geometric conversion |

: **What one lookup answers, and what clearance costs**: Reads for a sphere hull of radius `{python} RepresentationQuery.r_hull_str` plus the protective clearance, at a 5 cm pitch, against a budget of `{python} RepresentationQuery.reads_budget_str` reads per query on the permission controller. The octree count is the worst case near surfaces, a tree depth of `{python} RepresentationQuery.depth5_str` levels per cell; pruning reduces it in open space. {#tbl-09-representation-queries tbl-colwidths="[20,32,16,32]"}

::: {#fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Clearance query cost and snapshot storage by representation family**: (a) Memory reads to certify one sphere hull's clearance, computed from voxel pitch, hull radius plus protective clearance, and tree depth, against the per-query read budget that the 2 µs allocation and the permission controller's SRAM bandwidth allow. Occupancy scans grow with the cube of the inverse pitch and fit only at the coarsest pitch; an ESDF answers with one interpolated lookup at every pitch. (b) Storage for a dense snapshot of the stopping corridor (aisle width by clear distance by a chosen 2 m height) against the controller's SRAM. Counts, not measured latencies; rendering representations are absent because they do not answer a clearance query." fig-alt="Two log-scale panels against voxel pitch of 2, 5, and 10 cm. Panel a, memory reads per sphere-hull clearance query: worst-case octree scan from about 200,000 to about 1,300 reads, dense occupancy scan from about 22,000 to 180 reads, and ESDF lookup flat at 8 reads, with a dashed read budget at 800 per query that only the ESDF clears at every pitch and the occupancy scan clears only at 10 cm. Panel b, snapshot storage in kilobytes: ESDF at 8 bytes per cell falls from about 2,900 kB to 23 kB and occupancy at 4 bytes per cell from about 1,400 kB to 11 kB, with a dashed line at the permission MCU SRAM of about 1 MB that both snapshots exceed at 2 cm and fit under at 5 and 10 cm."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLEARANCE QUERY COST AND SNAPSHOT STORAGE (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto
# │ Goal:    show which representation answers a sphere-hull clearance query
# │          inside the per-query read budget, and which pitch fits the
# │          permission MCU's SRAM
# │ Show:    reads per query vs pitch (occupancy scan, octree scan, ESDF);
# │          snapshot storage vs pitch against SRAM capacity
# │ How:     all values from the RepresentationQuery cell
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
RQ = RepresentationQuery
PITCH = list(RQ.pitches_cm)  # cm, category: chosen (as in the cell)
OCC = [RQ.rows[p]["occ_reads"] for p in PITCH]
OCT = [RQ.rows[p]["oct_reads"] for p in PITCH]
ESDF = [RQ.rows[p]["esdf_reads"] for p in PITCH]
ESDF_KB = [RQ.rows[p]["esdf_bytes"].to(ureg.kilobyte).magnitude for p in PITCH]
OCC_KB = [RQ.rows[p]["occ_bytes"].to(ureg.kilobyte).magnitude for p in PITCH]
BUDGET = RQ.reads_budget
SRAM_KB = RQ.sram_cap.to(ureg.kilobyte).magnitude

# ┌── 2. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
viz.set_book_style()
C = viz.COLORS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5))

ax1.plot(PITCH, OCT, marker="s", lw=2, color=C["OrangeLine"], label="octree occupancy scan (worst case)")
ax1.plot(PITCH, OCC, marker="o", lw=2, color=C["RedLine"], label="dense occupancy scan")
ax1.plot(PITCH, ESDF, marker="^", lw=2, color=C["BlueLine"], label="ESDF lookup (trilinear)")
ax1.axhline(BUDGET, color=C["primary"], lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 4)))
ax1.text(1.7, BUDGET * 0.6, f"read budget: {BUDGET:.0f} per query", ha="left", va="top", fontsize=9, color=C["primary"])
ax1.set_yscale("log")
ax1.set_xticks(PITCH)
ax1.set_xlim(1.5, 10.5)
ax1.set_ylim(3, 1e6)
ax1.set_xlabel("Voxel pitch (cm)")
ax1.set_ylabel("Memory reads per sphere-hull query")
ax1.set_title("(a) Clearance query cost", loc="left", fontsize=11)
ax1.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8.5)

ax2.plot(PITCH, ESDF_KB, marker="^", lw=2, color=C["BlueLine"], label="ESDF snapshot, 8 B per cell")
ax2.plot(PITCH, OCC_KB, marker="o", lw=2, color=C["RedLine"], ls=(0, (6, 3)), label="occupancy snapshot, 4 B per cell")
ax2.axhline(SRAM_KB, color=C["primary"], lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 4)))
ax2.text(10.1, SRAM_KB * 1.25, "permission MCU SRAM", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=C["primary"])
ax2.set_yscale("log")
ax2.set_xticks(PITCH)
ax2.set_xlim(1.5, 10.5)
ax2.set_ylim(5, 2e4)
ax2.set_xlabel("Voxel pitch (cm)")
ax2.set_ylabel("Snapshot storage (kB)")
ax2.set_title("(b) Stopping-corridor snapshot", loc="left", fontsize=11)
ax2.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The counts in @fig-09-memory-3d-representation-pareto make the choice without any stipulated latency. A dense occupancy scan misses the read budget at 2 and 5 cm and fits only at 10 cm, where quantization alone, up to half a cell diagonal or `{python} RepresentationQuery.quant10_str`, consumes most of the protective clearance. A worst-case octree scan misses at every pitch, because each cell costs a descent. The ESDF answers with the same `{python} RepresentationQuery.esdf_reads_str` reads at every pitch, which is why it is the local snapshot's representation: its per-query cost does not grow as the pitch shrinks, and its storage becomes the binding constraint instead. A dense ESDF snapshot of the stopping corridor, the aisle width by the clear distance by a chosen `{python} RepresentationQuery.h_slab_str` height, or `{python} RepresentationQuery.v_slab_str`, needs `{python} RepresentationQuery.esdf5_bytes_str` at 5 cm and fits the controller's `{python} RepresentationQuery.sram_cap_str` of SRAM, while at 2 cm it needs `{python} RepresentationQuery.esdf2_bytes_str` and does not. The 5 cm pitch then charges up to `{python} RepresentationQuery.quant5_str` of quantization to the geometric error of every lookup, a cost the clearance check must subtract. A TSDF's projective distance cannot substitute for Euclidean clearance merely because its lookup is cheap.

The host maintains the larger reconstruction and prepares a bounded region covering the admitted motion and its fallback. The permission controller accepts a snapshot only when its provenance, geometry bounds, per-region evidence ages, and coverage satisfy the qualified interface. Snapshot construction, transfer, and admission consume time and memory of their own; @sec-placement must place and qualify that work separately from the local query. If the host stalls, the existing snapshot keeps aging. Motion can continue only while its own evidence, coverage, and fallback remain valid.

#### Volumetric memory footprint scaling {.unnumbered}

The local decision leaves the host with a capacity and update problem. Keeping the chosen snapshot supplied requires enough memory for the underlying map and enough bandwidth to integrate observations before their evidence expires.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-hashed-voxel-payload
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ILLUSTRATIVE HOST MAP SIZING: DENSE GRID VERSUS HASHED NARROW BAND
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps, host capacity calculation.
# │
# │ Goal:    Separate a dense workcell grid from a hashed surface band, and
# │          voxel payload from total allocated storage.
# │ Show:    dense grid bytes; band volume; block count; hashed payload.
# │ How:     M_dense = V / r^3 x S; V_band = 2 delta A; N_blocks = V_band /
# │          (B r)^3; payload = N_blocks x B^3 x S.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_memory, fmt_qty, fmt_qty_int, fmt_sci, check

class HashedVoxelPayload:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    l_x = 10.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (workcell length)
    l_y = 10.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (workcell width)
    l_z = 3.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (workcell height)
    pitch = 0.01 * ureg.meter  # category: chosen (manipulation resolution)
    voxel_bytes = 8 * ureg.byte  # category: illustrative (distance, weight, epoch payload)
    a_surface = 120.0 * ureg.meter**2  # category: illustrative (obstacle surface area in the workcell)
    delta_band = 0.04 * ureg.meter  # category: chosen (truncation band half-width)
    block_side = 8  # category: illustrative (voxels per block edge, the nvblox layout)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_ws = (l_x * l_y * l_z).to(ureg.meter**3)
    n_dense = (v_ws / pitch**3).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    m_dense = (n_dense * voxel_bytes).to(ureg.gigabyte)
    v_band = (2 * delta_band * a_surface).to(ureg.meter**3)
    blocks = (v_band / (block_side * pitch) ** 3).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    payload = (blocks * block_side**3 * voxel_bytes).to(ureg.megabyte)
    block_bytes = (block_side**3 * voxel_bytes).to(ureg.byte)
    band_fraction = (v_band / v_ws).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(m_dense.magnitude - 2.4) < 1e-9, f"Dense grid should be 2.4 GB, got {m_dense}.")
    check(abs(v_band.magnitude - 9.6) < 1e-9, f"Band volume should be 9.6 m^3, got {v_band}.")
    check(abs(blocks - 18_750) < 1e-6, f"Block count should be 18,750, got {blocks}.")
    check(abs(payload.magnitude - 76.8) < 1e-9, "Voxel payload is 76.8 MB before overhead.")
    check(abs(block_bytes.magnitude - 4096) < 1e-9, "One 8^3 block of 8 B voxels is 4,096 B.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_ws_str = fmt_qty_int(v_ws, ureg.meter**3)
    pitch_str = fmt_length(pitch, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    voxel_bytes_str = fmt_int(voxel_bytes.magnitude)
    n_dense_str = fmt_sci(n_dense, precision=0)
    m_dense_str = fmt_memory(m_dense, unit=ureg.gigabyte, precision=1)
    a_surface_str = fmt_qty_int(a_surface, ureg.meter**2)
    delta_band_str = fmt_length(delta_band, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    v_band_str = fmt_qty(v_band, ureg.meter**3, precision=1)
    blocks_str = fmt_int(blocks)
    payload_str = fmt_memory(payload, unit=ureg.megabyte, precision=1)
    block_bytes_str = fmt_int(block_bytes.magnitude)
    band_pct_str = fmt_percent(band_fraction, precision=1, style="prose")
```

For the illustrative host-map sizing calculation, consider an operational workspace of physical volume $V_{\text{ws}} = L_x L_y L_z$. Discretizing this domain into cubic voxels of uniform pitch $r$ requires memory proportional to workspace volume and to the inverse cube of voxel width:
$$M_{\text{dense}} = \left(\frac{V_{\text{ws}}}{r^3}\right) S_{\text{voxel}}$$ {#eq-mem-footprint-dense}
where $S_{\text{voxel}}$ represents the storage footprint per voxel, here `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.voxel_bytes_str` bytes: 4 for a 32-bit distance, 2 for the observation weight, and 2 for the evidence epoch. For a warehouse workcell of 10 m by 10 m by 3 m, `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.v_ws_str`, at a manipulation resolution of `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.pitch_str`, @eq-mem-footprint-dense gives `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.n_dense_str` voxels and `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.m_dense_str` of contiguous DRAM, most of it describing empty air. On an embedded robot computer, that allocation competes directly with the vision backbone and the controllers.

Obstacles occupy thin surfaces, not volumes, and a TSDF needs values only near them. Truncating the distance field to a band $[-\delta, +\delta]$ around observed surfaces restricts storage to a shell $V_{\text{band}} \approx 2\delta \cdot A_{\text{surface}}$, where $A_{\text{surface}}$ is the total obstacle surface area. Partitioning space into blocks of $B^3$ voxels with block pitch $L_B = B \cdot r$, and allocating a block only when it holds data, the sparse hashed footprint obeys:
$$M_{\text{hashed}} = N_{\text{blocks}} \left( B^3 S_{\text{voxel}} + S_{\text{meta}} \right) + N_{\text{buckets}} S_{\text{entry}}$$ {#eq-mem-footprint-hashed}
where $N_{\text{blocks}} \approx \lceil 2\delta A_{\text{surface}} / (B r)^3 \rceil$, $S_{\text{meta}}$ is the block metadata (coordinates, allocation flags), and $S_{\text{entry}}$ is the hash-table entry size. With an illustrative `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.a_surface_str` of obstacle surface in the same workcell and $\delta$ = `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.delta_band_str`, the band is `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.v_band_str`, `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.band_pct_str` of the workcell, which by @eq-mem-footprint-hashed with $B = 8$ takes about `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.blocks_str` blocks and `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.payload_str` of voxel payload. Total allocation adds block metadata, hash entries, and the partially filled blocks at band boundaries, so the payload is a lower bound on map memory, not an upper one.

The narrow-band estimate describes a TSDF, not the ESDF the snapshot needs. An ESDF stores a distance wherever a clearance may be queried, which means over the observed free volume out to its maximum distance, so its footprint scales with $V_{\text{obs}}/r^3$ rather than with surface area; for an aisle machine that volume is the corridor the machine can reach, which is why the snapshot above was sized from the corridor. Allocation also carries meaning. When ray integration allocates every block a sensor ray crosses, as free-space carving does, an unallocated block is one no ray has reached and can be read as unknown. When only the surface band is allocated, an unallocated block may be observed free space, and the map must mark observation separately. A permission-grade map therefore distinguishes three states explicitly rather than inferring them from allocation: observed free with a live evidence epoch, unknown, and expired, meaning observed once but older than its horizon.

#### Voxel block hashing index mapping {.unnumbered}

Sparse allocation needs an index that finds a block without the pointer chains of an octree. **Voxel block hashing**\index{Voxel block hashing} maps continuous world coordinates $\mathbf{x} = [x, y, z]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3$ to an integer block index $\mathbf{u} = [u_x, u_y, u_z]^\top \in \mathbb{Z}^3$:
$$\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) = \left\lfloor \frac{\mathbf{x}}{B \cdot r} \right\rfloor$$ {#eq-mem-block-index}
and a spatial hash then resolves the index of @eq-mem-block-index to a table bucket $h(\mathbf{u}) \in \{0, \dots, N_{\text{buckets}}-1\}$.[^fn-algo-voxel-hashing] The scheme was introduced for large-scale real-time reconstruction by @niessner2013real, using the spatial hash of @teschner2003optimized, and it underlies robotic mapping libraries such as Voxblox and nvblox [@oleynikova2017voxblox; @millane2024nvblox]. In the nvblox layout of $8^3$ voxels per block, an 8-byte voxel makes each block `{python} HashedVoxelPayload.block_bytes_str` bytes laid out contiguously, so one hash lookup brings a whole neighborhood into the same memory region. Retrieval is expected $O(1)$, but hash collisions, probe length, cold caches, and concurrent updates all lengthen the worst case, so expected complexity cannot replace a measured bound for the local permission query; the snapshot above avoids the question by being dense.

[^fn-algo-voxel-hashing]: **Spatial hashing and voxel offsets**\index{Voxel block hashing!spatial hash}: The hash of @teschner2003optimized, adopted by @niessner2013real, computes $h(\mathbf{u}) = (u_x p_1 \oplus u_y p_2 \oplus u_z p_3) \bmod N_{\text{buckets}}$ with the primes $p_1 = 73{,}856{,}093$, $p_2 = 19{,}349{,}663$, and $p_3 = 83{,}492{,}791$. Implementations differ; Voxblox, for example, uses a linear combination of the block coordinates instead. Within a block, the voxel offset is $\Delta \mathbf{u} = \lfloor \mathbf{x}/r \rfloor - B \mathbf{u}$, stored linearly at $\Delta u_x + B(\Delta u_y + B\,\Delta u_z)$.

#### DRAM update bandwidth during ray marching {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-raymarch-bandwidth
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NAIVE RAY-MARCHING UPDATE TRAFFIC
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps (@eq-mem-dram-bandwidth).
# │
# │ Goal:    Price one depth stream's naive map-update traffic and compare it
# │          with the host SoC's registered peak DRAM bandwidth.
# │ Show:    rays per frame, steps per ray, traffic, share of peak.
# │ How:     BW = f_cam x N_rays x (d_ray / r) x S_rw.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty_int

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class RaymarchBandwidth:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    width_px = 640  # category: illustrative (VGA depth stream)
    height_px = 480  # category: illustrative (VGA depth stream)
    f_cam = 30 * ureg.hertz  # category: illustrative (depth frame rate)
    d_ray = 2.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative (mean marched distance)
    pitch = 0.02 * ureg.meter  # category: chosen (voxel pitch)
    s_rw = 8 * ureg.byte  # category: illustrative (read-modify-write traffic per voxel, low end)
    soc_bw = RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet (host SoC peak DRAM bandwidth)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_rays = width_px * height_px
    n_steps = (d_ray / pitch).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    bw = (f_cam * n_rays * n_steps * s_rw).to(ureg.gigabyte / ureg.second)
    share = (bw / soc_bw).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(bw.magnitude - 7.3728) < 1e-6, f"Ray-march traffic should be 7.37 GB/s, got {bw}.")
    check(share < 0.05, "One naive depth stream should take under 5 percent of peak.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_rays_str = fmt_int(n_rays)
    f_cam_str = fmt_qty_int(f_cam, ureg.hertz)
    d_ray_str = fmt_length(d_ray, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    pitch_str = fmt_length(pitch, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    n_steps_str = fmt_int(n_steps)
    bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw, unit=ureg.gigabyte / ureg.second, precision=2)
    soc_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(soc_bw, unit=ureg.gigabyte / ureg.second, precision=0)
    share_str = fmt_percent(share, precision=1, style="prose")
```

When depth cameras stream range frames at framerate $f_{\text{cam}}$ with $N_{\text{rays}} = W \times H$ pixels per frame, updating the volumetric map requires ray marching from the sensor origin to each observed surface point [@curless1996volumetric]. Each ray traverses a line-of-sight distance $d_{\text{ray}}$ at voxel stepping pitch $r$, requiring $N_{\text{steps}} = d_{\text{ray}} / r$ discrete cell evaluations. The raw DRAM update bandwidth consumed by naive ray marching is:
$$\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}} = f_{\text{cam}} \cdot N_{\text{rays}} \cdot \left(\frac{d_{\text{ray}}}{r}\right) \cdot S_{\text{rw}}$$ {#eq-mem-dram-bandwidth}
where $S_{\text{rw}}$ is the read-modify-write memory traffic per traversed voxel (8 to 16 bytes for reading the current occupancy or distance, updating running weights, and writing back).
