For an illustrative VGA depth stream of `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.n_rays_str` rays at `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.f_cam_str`, marched over `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.d_ray_str` at a `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.pitch_str` pitch (`{python} RaymarchBandwidth.n_steps_str` steps per ray) with 8 bytes per step, @eq-mem-dram-bandwidth gives `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.bw_str`, `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.share_str` of the peak `{python} RaymarchBandwidth.soc_bw_str` of the host system-on-chip (SoC). The share of peak understates the effect, because these map updates share the memory system with the vision model and other workloads, and their cost depends on access locality and competing traffic rather than on peak bandwidth. The update calculation identifies a load to include in the contention test; it does not establish a measured interference bound. Block hashing reduces this traffic by keeping active blocks in on-chip memory, and projective TSDF updates project voxels inside the viewing frustum onto the depth image instead of marching every ray. These methods reduce repeated memory traffic, but the reduction depends on scene coverage and update strategy. Sparse allocation still grows as the machine explores new regions; a bounded host store needs an explicit retention policy.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_volumetric_raycasting_bandwidth_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical ladder comparing SoC bus limit against dense TSDF and sparse VDB memory bandwidth."}
*Dense voxel updates consume shared memory bandwidth; sparse updates reduce that traffic but still require contention tests.*
:::

What a map can certify comes from how a range return updates it. Traversing the ray from the sensor to the return [@amanatides1987fast], the map asserts **negative evidence**\index{Negative evidence} in every cell the ray crossed and positive evidence in the cell where it ended; @sec-appendix-ml-voxels gives the log-odds update. A valid empty ray can retire a phantom obstacle, but it says nothing about the volume behind a return. A new scan down the aisle therefore cannot renew cells hidden behind the rack. Sparse allocation saves capacity without eliminating ray traversal, and any resulting processing delay adds to evidence age (@sec-placement-resource-contention).

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_active_negative_evidence_chain.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Causal chain showing raycast through free space to surface hit, evicting ghost obstacles."}

*Active negative evidence along sightlines clears phantom obstacles without waiting for timeout decay.*
:::

Because negative evidence renews only the cells a ray crossed, a map's publication time dates none of its cells. The manifest in @tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief therefore carries cell evidence epochs alongside occupancy. For the worked local snapshot, checking a hull includes the supporting cells' evidence and unknown-space status within the allocated query time. A freshly copied distance value with expired source cells cannot establish clearance. The manifest travels with the bounded snapshot as well as the host map; the isolated controller does not traverse the full host store.

These pieces combine into the one quantity the permission path needs from a map. Build the snapshot ESDF with every occupied, unknown, or expired cell treated as an obstacle. Its value at a hull center, minus the hull radius, is then the **free-space depth**\index{Free-space depth} $d_{\text{free}}$: the distance from the hull's surface to the nearest place that no live evidence vouches for. A person, a tote, or anything else the sensors cannot currently see can only be beyond that boundary, so $d_{\text{free}}$ is exactly what motion may spend. For a candidate aisle advance, the consumer subtracts the geometric error, including quantization and localization, and the protective clearance from $d_{\text{free}}$; if the remainder is positive the query passes. When the nearest boundary is the occluded cross aisle, $d_{\text{free}}$ is small however fast the lookup, and a small numerical query latency cannot rescue the claim. How quickly the remainder shrinks while the sensors cannot see that boundary is the subject of @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion.

#### Map maintenance: Forgetting, decay, and change {.unnumbered}

A map built for a warehouse must also forget. Totes move, doors swing, and people walk through cells the sensors saw empty a minute ago, so a map that keeps every observation forever accumulates phantom obstacles where objects left and phantom free space where they arrived unseen. Negative evidence handles the first case whenever a ray passes through the cell again. The second case has no ray to correct it, and the practical mechanisms differ in what they assume about the cells nobody is looking at.

@Tbl-09-map-maintenance sets out the mechanisms in current use. Two of them are old and structural. OctoMap clamps each cell's log-odds between fixed bounds, so that a cell observed occupied a thousand times can still be cleared by a few contradicting rays; clamping keeps the map able to change, but it acts only on cells that are observed again [@hornung2013octomap]. Independent Markov chain occupancy grids give every cell a two-state transition model whose entry and exit rates are learned online, so an unobserved cell's occupancy relaxes toward its learned long-run value [@saarinen2012independent]. The recent systems move the same ideas to GPU maps and to objects. The nvblox library decays the occupancy probability of voxels that have left the field of view toward 0.5, the unknown state, at a fixed frequency, which relaxes the assumption that an occupancy map holds only static structure [@millane2024nvblox; @nvidia2026nvbloxdocs]. Dynablox detects moving objects by incrementally estimating high-confidence free space and flagging returns that appear inside it [@schmid2023dynablox]. Khronos separates a fast process that tracks short-term dynamics within an active window from a slower factor-graph process that reasons about long-term changes to the scene [@schmid2024khronos].

Each of these is a rate model: it states how an unobserved cell is expected to change, calibrated from past traffic or tuned by hand. The permission path needs the worst case instead. The deterministic expiry this chapter derives is that worst-case twin: a free cell becomes unknown no later than the time at which something moving at the site's speed bound could have entered it from the nearest unobserved boundary. A decay rate is safe for permission only if it reaches the unknown state no later than that bound; otherwise it is a useful expectation for the planner, not evidence for the permission path.

| Mechanism                           | What happens to a cell nobody observes                               | Representative system (as of 2026) | What it cannot certify                            |
|:------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| Clamped log-odds                    | Nothing; clamping only speeds change when the cell is seen again     | OctoMap                            | Any change in cells no ray reaches                |
| Per-cell transition model           | Occupancy relaxes toward a learned long-run value                    | Independent Markov chain grids     | A worst case; learned rates describe past traffic |
| Decay toward unknown                | Occupancy relaxes toward 0.5 at a fixed rate once out of view        | nvblox                             | Safety, unless the rate is set from a speed bound |
| Dynamic-object detection            | Unchanged; returns inside confident free space are flagged as moving | Dynablox                           | Objects the sensors do not currently see          |
| Spatio-temporal SLAM                | Unchanged until revisited; change is detected on reobservation       | Khronos                            | The interval between visits                       |
| Deterministic expiry (this chapter) | Free becomes unknown at the erosion deadline set by the speed bound  | Worked design                      | Nothing past the deadline, by construction        |

: **Map maintenance mechanisms and what they certify, as of 2026**: Rate models describe expected change and serve planning; only an expiry derived from a speed bound certifies that an unobserved cell is still free. The named systems are point-in-time implementations of each mechanism. {#tbl-09-map-maintenance tbl-colwidths="[20,32,18,30]"}

| Map field                                 | Unit or type                         | Meaning and consumer check                                                                                          |
|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `voxel_grid_origin`, `voxel_resolution_m` | m; m                                 | Spatial anchor and pitch; match the active frame and calibration                                                    |
| `pose_graph_revision`                     | integer                              | Revision of the pose graph that placed the cells; a loop closure that changes it re-anchors or expires the snapshot |
| `map_update_epoch`                        | capture-clock ns                     | Last map publication/update; **not** freshness of every cell                                                        |
| `cell_evidence_epoch`                     | capture-clock ns per cell            | Last physical observation for that cell; never refreshed by prediction or unrelated map updates                     |
| `free_space_sweep_epoch`                  | capture-clock ns per occupancy cell  | Last valid observed free ray through that cell                                                                      |
| `cell_state`                              | free, unknown, or expired per cell   | Set explicitly, never inferred from allocation; unknown and expired read as obstacles                               |
| `clock_conversion`, `sync_error_ns`       | mapping; ns                          | Convert capture epochs to the consumer's monotonic clock with bounded error                                         |
| `query_latency_budget_us`                 | $\mu\text{s}$ ($\le 2\ \mu\text{s}$) | Bound collision and distance gradient query time to preserve 1 kHz reactive control loops                           |

: **Volumetric belief manifest and cell evidence**: The map header describes layout, pose-graph revision, query latency budget, and update time, while cell-local acquisition epochs and states determine whether the particular path region is fresh. The consumer treats unobserved or expired cells as unknown unless a separately validated policy permits traversal. {#tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief tbl-colwidths="[26,22,52]"}

### Hierarchical 3D dynamic scene graphs {#sec-memory-hierarchical-scene-graphs}

Semantic memory sits above the metric layer and inherits its limits. @Sec-perception-error-clearance introduced the object-centric 3D scene graph as something perception produces; memory has to keep one. The structure descends from the 3D scene graph of @armeni20193d, which organized a building into layers of objects, rooms, and cameras, and the 3D dynamic scene graph of @rosinol20203d, which added places, agents, and their motion; Kimera and Hydra build such graphs incrementally from a robot's sensor stream [@rosinol2021kimera; @hughes2022hydra]. @Fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph shows the layers, from a metric mesh through objects and agents, places, and rooms to the building.

::: {#fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Hierarchical 3D dynamic scene graph architecture**: Five-layer spatio-temporal memory organization bridging continuous 3D-indexed metric state stores to symbolic foundation reasoning. Layer 1 captures triangular metric mesh geometry; Layer 2 extracts 3D objects and dynamic agents; Layer 3 models topological places via Voronoi freespace clearance spheres ($p_i$); Layer 4 structures architectural rooms and portals; and Layer 5 establishes global building mission topology. Vertical inter-layer edges coordinate upward abstraction (compressing metric surfaces into symbolic entities) and downward grounding (translating task tokens into metric coordinates) (adapted from Rosinol et al. [@rosinol20203d; @rosinol2021kimera] and Hughes et al. [@hughes2022hydra])." fig-alt="Hierarchical five-layer 3D Dynamic Scene Graph architecture. From bottom to top: Layer 1 Metric Mesh surface geometry, Layer 2 Objects and Agents with support relations, Layer 3 Places with Voronoi freespace clearance spheres, Layer 4 Rooms connected by portals, and Layer 5 Buildings with global topology. Side arrows depict upward Abstraction and downward Grounding across tiers."}
![](images/svg/fig09_dynamic_scene_graph_hierarchy.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The inter-layer edges in @fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph let a policy reason over objects and places without repeatedly processing the full metric mesh. In the opposite direction, a request for the latch handle resolves through the graph to an object frame and the geometry needed for a candidate approach. For memory, the question is what ages in a node, and three things age at different rates. A node's pose ages at the speed bound of what it describes: the bolted rack not at all, a tote on a cart at walking speed. Its existence ages independently of its pose, because an object can leave while unseen, and a tight pose covariance says nothing about whether it is still there (@sec-memory-fallacies-pitfalls). Its label comes from a learned model and does not decay physically, but it is only as reliable as that model's calibration and is revisited only on reobservation. Current systems update graphs when the sensors return: Hydra corrects the graph when the underlying trajectory is optimized after a loop closure [@hughes2022hydra], and Khronos detects objects that have changed or disappeared when it revisits them [@schmid2024khronos]. Neither ages an unobserved node by a physical bound, so that remains the belief record's job, and a room or object label cannot renew the age of the metric cells beneath it.

### Episodic memory and physical interaction history {#sec-memory-episodic}

Metric maps and scene graphs answer *where* objects and free space are. **Episodic memory**\index{Episodic memory} answers *what happened*: the contact events, gripper transitions, stalls, and interventions of a task, indexed by their capture epochs so a later step can ask whether the latch was already released or the tote already placed. A learned policy can retrieve this history without making its context the authoritative state store. A **streaming window**\index{Streaming ring-buffer attention} bounds attention storage by evicting older tokens [@xiao2024streamingllm], whether or not their physical consequences have ended; a closed latch observed a hundred navigation steps ago is exactly the kind of token such a window drops. The metric record and the event anchors must therefore outlive context eviction when they still constrain the task. Retrieval gives the policy relevant geometry and history; the spatial belief record supplies the evidence age and bound that a motion consumer can check.

For motion permission, then, a representation without an epoch is an unverified assertion, and an estimate whose error bound exceeds task tolerance must be excluded from motion proposals before the permission path considers actuator commands. The machine cannot halt every operation at the first missed frame, however. Extending action across brief sensing gaps requires estimators that propagate belief forward until new measurements arrive to confirm or correct the state.

## Forward State Propagation and Occlusion Decay {#sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion}

When a sensor loses sight of a moving body, stopping also takes time and requires a usable state estimate. Forward propagation carries the last observation across that interval, whether the machine continues a permitted task or executes a fallback. A learned generative model can also predict future trajectories autoregressively\index{Network!autoregressive}, and ensembles or sampled rollouts give it a spread of predictions, but that spread is not a qualified bound on physical error. In physical AI, forward propagation must be coupled to explicit error-growth models—whether implemented via recursive continuous-discrete Kalman filters [@kalman1960new], learned stochastic state observers, or expanding 3D Gaussian covariance ellipsoids.[^fn-hist-bayesian-filter]

Forward propagation changes the estimate and its uncertainty while preserving the hardware evidence epoch. Across the blind interval, anticipated motion remains useful only while the growing error fits the task's clearance. The rack-end example makes that limit explicit.

[^fn-hist-bayesian-filter]: **Bayesian state estimation provenance**\index{State estimation!Bayesian provenance}: @kalman1960new introduced recursive minimum mean-square error state estimation for linear dynamic systems. @moravec1985high generalized these recursive Bayesian updates to spatial occupancy grids, modeling sensor beam uncertainty through explicit range-bearing distributions. In embodied systems, uncompensated propagation across extended sensor dropouts causes Bayesian belief distributions to disperse, requiring explicit invalidation horizons to prevent open-loop control divergence.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-rack-end-belief
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RACK-END FREE SPACE THROUGH OCCLUSION (EROSION LAW)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion (free-space erosion, the
# │          walking-person term, worked roots, the expiry table, the
# │          skewed-record pitfall), @sec-memory-summary.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that memory certifies the aisle only to a depth set by the
# │          distance from the occlusion boundary: nothing beside the rack
# │          end, a useful interval in the open aisle ahead.
# │ Show:    the erosion deadline abreast of the rack end (side clearance) and
# │          for the aisle ahead (clear distance); what the frame's age leaves
# │          of the second; the running total memory leaves unchanged; the
# │          walking-person term at the drive limit against the clear distance.
# │ How:     calc_free_space_expiry: max(0, (d_free - dloc - dmargin) / v_h); the
# │          running total from the RM/AISLE terms at the drive limit; the
# │          walking term v_h (tau_delay + v / a_brake) for a constant-
# │          deceleration stop at the drive limit (the C2 suffix is Ch11's, and
# │          the speed ceiling this term implies is computed in Ch12).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_free_space_expiry

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class RackEndBelief:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative (localization bound)
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen (protective clearance)
    v_h = AISLE.v_human_approach  # category: datasheet (ISO 13855 walking speed)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance; free depth ahead)
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative (hull-to-rack gap; free depth abreast of the rack end)
    frame_rate = RM.nav_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet (navigation camera)
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived (@sec-perception-transduction-calibration)
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible deceleration)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (total pre-brake delay)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_exp_abreast = calc_free_space_expiry(side_clearance, delta_loc, delta_margin, v_h).to(millisecond)
    t_exp_ahead = calc_free_space_expiry(d_clear, delta_loc, delta_margin, v_h).to(millisecond)
    t_left_at_dispatch = (t_exp_ahead - t_age).to(millisecond)
    frame_period = (1 / frame_rate).to(millisecond)
    frames_bridged = (t_left_at_dispatch / frame_period).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    d_age_eroded = (v_h * t_age).to(ureg.millimeter)
    slack_abreast = (side_clearance - delta_loc - delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # rows 1-5 of the stopping budget at the drive limit (Ch2, Ch4, Ch8 terms)
    running_total = calc_safe_stopping_distance(
        v_drive,
        AISLE.t_brake_onset + AISLE.t_lease + AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + t_age,
        a_brake,
        delta_loc,
        delta_margin,
    ).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # walking person: a person approaching at v_h for the whole stop adds
    # v_h (tau_delay + T_stop); at the drive limit with a constant-deceleration
    # stop, T_stop = v / a_brake.
    t_stop_const = (v_drive / a_brake).to(ureg.second)
    d_walk_term = (v_h * (tau_delay + t_stop_const)).to(ureg.meter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(slack_abreast.magnitude) < 1e-9, f"Abreast of the rack end the free depth should be exactly spent, got {slack_abreast}.")
    check(t_exp_abreast.magnitude == 0.0, f"Memory must certify nothing abreast of the rack end, got {t_exp_abreast}.")
    check(abs(t_exp_ahead.magnitude - 593.75) < 1e-9, f"Aisle-ahead expiry should be 593.75 ms, got {t_exp_ahead}.")
    check(t_left_at_dispatch > 10 * frame_period, "The aisle-ahead claim must outlast many camera frames after dispatch.")
    check(abs(t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 1e-9, f"Observation age should be 51.6 ms, got {t_age}.")
    check(abs(running_total.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 912.9) < 5e-3, f"Running total after Ch8 should be 912.9 mm, got {running_total}.")
    check(abs(d_walk_term.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 1.41) < 5e-3, f"Walking term at the drive limit should be 1.41 m, got {d_walk_term}.")
    check(d_walk_term > d_clear, "The walking term alone must exceed the rack-end clear distance.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_margin_str = fmt_length(delta_margin, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    v_h_str = fmt_velocity(v_h, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    side_clearance_str = fmt_length(side_clearance, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    t_exp_abreast_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_abreast, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_ahead_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_ahead, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    t_left_str = fmt_latency(t_left_at_dispatch, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    frames_bridged_str = fmt_int(frames_bridged)
    d_age_eroded_str = fmt_length(d_age_eroded, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    frame_period_str = fmt_latency(frame_period, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    running_total_str = fmt_length(running_total, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive, precision=1)
    d_walk_term_str = fmt_length(d_walk_term, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
```

The difference between predicting a state and observing it decides what the machine may do at the rack end. A person can step out there into the illustrative `{python} RackEndBelief.d_clear_str` clear distance $D_{\text{clear}}$ that the stopping budget defends, and once the rack hides the cross aisle, the question is how long the remembered view may vouch that the machine's surroundings are still empty.

Every physical model simplifies reality, causing error between the projected state and the physical world to expand continuously during the blind interval. In state estimation\index{State estimation}, this dispersion is governed by **occlusion covariance expansion**\index{Occlusion covariance expansion}, the continuous, physics-governed widening of uncertainty during sensor line-of-sight dropouts. Mathematically formalized by stochastic models (such as the continuous Lyapunov/Riccati covariance propagation equation, detailed in @sec-appendix-control-covariance), this expansion quantifies the growing doubt about where an object actually is, bounding the unobserved divergence caused by unknown drift velocities and unexpected physical disturbances before the sensor regains visibility. For a deterministic worked model, suppose sensor characterization and disturbance limits establish an initial position-error bound $E_0$ at the moment of occlusion ($\Delta t = 0$). Two bounded terms then degrade the prediction. Motion the model does not know about introduces a drift velocity bounded by $v_{\text{drift}}$, and forces it does not model create a disturbance acceleration bounded by $a_{\text{dist}}$. Over an occlusion duration $\Delta t$, the error bound $E(\Delta t)$ then follows the quadratic expansion:

$$E(\Delta t) = E_0 + v_{\text{drift}}\Delta t + \frac{1}{2}a_{\text{dist}}(\Delta t)^2$$ {#eq-mem-occlusion-expansion}

At the rack end the stored belief is not the position of a tracked object but a spatial claim: no person stands within the protective clearance $\delta_{\text{margin}}$, `{python} RackEndBelief.delta_margin_str`, of the machine. The map supports that claim to the free-space depth $d_{\text{free}}$ of @sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps, the distance from the hull to the nearest cell no live evidence vouches for, and anything the sensors cannot see lies beyond that boundary. Two terms spend that depth. The machine knows where it stands only to within the localization bound $\delta_{\text{loc}}$, `{python} RackEndBelief.delta_loc_str`, so the true gap may already be that much smaller, and a hidden person can advance from the boundary at up to the walking-speed bound $v_h$ of `{python} RackEndBelief.v_h_str` that safety-distance calculations assume for an approaching person. In the form of @eq-mem-occlusion-expansion, the error is $E(\Delta t) = \delta_{\text{loc}} + v_h\,\Delta t$ with $a_{\text{dist}} = 0$, and the tolerance is the depth the clearance does not need, $d_{\text{free}} - \delta_{\text{margin}}$. The free region therefore erodes from its unobserved boundary at walking speed, and the claim lapses at

$$T_{\text{inv}} = \frac{d_{\text{free}} - \delta_{\text{loc}} - \delta_{\text{margin}}}{v_h}$$ {#eq-mem-free-space-expiry}

evaluated for every hull the admitted motion and its stop will occupy, with a result of zero or less meaning that memory certifies nothing there. This **free-space erosion**\index{Free-space erosion} law is the worst-case form of the occlusion-aware reachable sets used in automated driving, where the region an unseen road user could occupy grows from the edge of the visible area [@orzechowski2018tackling].

The law gives two very different answers on the same aisle. Abreast of the rack end, the unobserved cross aisle begins at the upright itself, so $d_{\text{free}}$ is the `{python} RackEndBelief.side_clearance_str` side clearance between hull and rack, exactly what localization error and protective clearance together consume. The deadline is `{python} RackEndBelief.t_exp_abreast_str`: memory cannot certify that position even at the instant of capture, and no frame rate changes that. For a hull at the machine's current position, with the rack end `{python} RackEndBelief.d_clear_str` ahead as the nearest unobserved boundary, the same law allows `{python} RackEndBelief.t_exp_ahead_str`. The frame that saw the aisle empty is already `{python} RackEndBelief.t_age_str` old when perception dispatches it (@sec-perception-transduction-calibration), which erodes `{python} RackEndBelief.d_age_eroded_str` of that depth before memory receives it and leaves `{python} RackEndBelief.t_left_str`, about `{python} RackEndBelief.frames_bridged_str` frame periods of the navigation camera. In the open aisle, memory usefully bridges dropped frames. Memory certifies the aisle only to a depth set by the distance from the occlusion boundary, and at the rack end that depth is gone.

Nothing in the software marks the moment of expiry. The map still shows the cross aisle free, and the estimator still publishes a well-formed record, yet the prediction has stopped functioning as evidence. The eroded cells become unknown, and the region beside the rack end is unknown from the moment the uprights hide it. The stopping budget protects a static obstacle at $D_{\text{clear}}$, such as a person who has stepped out and stands in the aisle, or a dropped tote, and memory adds a deadline to that budget but no distance. The running total at the drive limit stays at the `{python} RackEndBelief.running_total_str` that @sec-perception-transduction-calibration left.

A person who keeps walking toward the machine during the whole stop is a different obstacle. A safety-distance calculation counts that approach as $v_h(\tau_{\text{delay}} + T_{\text{stop}})$, the walking speed applied over the entire time from detection to standstill. At the `{python} RackEndBelief.v_drive_str` drive limit, where a constant-deceleration stop lasts $T_{\text{stop}} = v/a_{\text{brake}}$, that term alone comes to `{python} RackEndBelief.d_walk_term_str`, more than the entire `{python} RackEndBelief.d_clear_str` clear distance before any other distance in the budget is counted. The static-clearance calculation therefore supports no unrestricted shared crossing. The proposed site restriction combines a marked crossing with rack-end presence sensing, but it remains a candidate control until detection coverage, response timing, and the site rule are qualified. Site operations owns that premise, retained in @sec-frontier-residual-claims-register; remembered emptiness cannot substitute for the missing evidence. Whatever crossing rule the site adopts, the permission path must refuse any proposal whose clearance relies on remembered emptiness past the belief's deadline.

::: {#dfn-memory-belief-invalidation-horizon .callout-definition title="Belief state invalidation horizon"}

***Belief state invalidation horizon***\index{Belief state invalidation horizon!definition}\index{Uncertainty!invalidation horizon} ($T_{\text{inv}}$) is the elapsed time since the last physical observation at which the belief's validated error bound $E(\Delta t)$ first reaches the task tolerance $E_{\max}$:
$$T_{\text{inv}} = \inf \{ \Delta t \ge 0 : E(\Delta t) \ge E_{\max} \}$$ {#eq-mem-invalidation-horizon}
where $E(\Delta t)$ is a bounded-disturbance growth law such as @eq-mem-occlusion-expansion or a calibrated error quantile, and a belief whose evidence epoch is $t_0$ stops supporting motion at $t_0 + T_{\text{inv}}$.

1.  **Significance**: Formalizes the hard mathematical boundary where forward-propagated state estimation ceases to function as valid physical evidence, requiring the permission path to refuse dependent motion proposals before geometric clearance is breached.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike open-loop timeout watchdogs that monitor software process heartbeat intervals, the invalidation horizon is derived from continuous physical kinematics, bounded disturbance dynamics, and mechanical clearance constraints.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Allowing a neural planner or Kalman filter to continuously extrapolate state estimates during extended sensor dropouts without bounding error expansion, mistaking smooth mathematical extrapolation for physical ground truth.

:::

When the growth law is linear, $E(\Delta t) = E_0 + r\,\Delta t$, the horizon has a closed form,
$$T_{\text{inv}} = \frac{E_{\max} - E_0}{r}$$ {#eq-mem-linear-horizon}
and a result of zero or less means the belief never supported the task. The free-space erosion law of @eq-mem-free-space-expiry is this form with $E_0 = \delta_{\text{loc}}$, $r = v_h$, and $E_{\max} = d_{\text{free}} - \delta_{\text{margin}}$; the mug-handle belief of @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema is the same form with the conveyor's speed, and the evidence horizon of an intent lease in @sec-intent applies it to the lease's target. This chapter owns the expiry law; later chapters apply it.

Reacquiring line of sight can restore useful evidence, but arrival alone is insufficient. The estimator computes the **innovation**\index{Innovation}, the difference between the new measurement and the predicted observation. A compatible measurement supports an update only after identity, calibration, and the relevant physical constraints have also been checked. A large residual may expose an outlier or a violated motion model; the estimator must resolve that discrepancy before renewing dependent authority. Updating the estimate does not authorize a discontinuous actuator target. The later force-and-bias example shows the complementary limit: a small residual cannot validate a state dimension the sensor does not observe.

Model prediction serves as a temporary bridge across missing or delayed observations, and the bridge holds only while the accumulated model error remains smaller than the mechanical tolerance of the task. How soon it fails depends on what drives the error. At the rack end a speed bound alone set the rate. At the cage door, the width of the latch-release slot sets the tolerance $E_{\max}$ for the gripper finger that must enter it, and unmodeled forces add terms that grow faster than any speed bound. Between sensor updates the estimator propagates the state by integrating commanded forces through its model of the plant, without feedback confirmation.

The stochastic model behind that propagation separates three mechanisms of decay. An unmeasured velocity error at the onset of occlusion grows position variance as $\sigma_v^2(0)(\Delta t)^2$, and unmodeled stochastic forces such as torque ripple or structural vibration, integrated twice, grow it as $\frac{1}{3}q_c(\Delta t)^3$\index{Mathematics!cubic variance expansion}; these variance terms are what a calibrated quantile must absorb. A steady unmodeled force bounded by $|a_{\text{dist}}|$, such as a dragging cable or persistent sliding friction, instead deflects the body by at most $\frac{1}{2}a_{\text{dist}}(\Delta t)^2$, the deterministic term of @eq-mem-occlusion-expansion.[^fn-math-nonsmooth-contact]

[^fn-math-nonsmooth-contact]: **Non-smooth contact dynamics**\index{Dynamics!non-smooth contact}: Physical surface contact introduces set-valued Coulomb friction and non-smooth stick-slip transitions that break linear covariance propagation models. Transitioning between stick and slip modes injects discontinuous velocity steps that invalidate continuous kinematic drift bounds. Managing these contact regime transitions requires hybrid state estimators that switch between distinct error growth matrices upon detecting normal force thresholds.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-latch-slot-belief
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LATCH-SLOT FINGER BELIEF
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion (quadratic root, tightened slot,
# │          constant-velocity overrun), @fig-uncertainty-growth (plot inputs),
# │          @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema (the filled belief record).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that unmodeled forces shorten a belief's life faster than
# │          tolerance shrinks, and fill the chapter's belief record on the
# │          machine's own arm.
# │ Show:    the invalidation horizon of the finger in the latch-release slot;
# │          the horizon for a tighter slot; what a constant-velocity estimator
# │          would admit; the clock-conversion bound the record carries.
# │ How:     E(t) = E0 + v_drift t + a_dist t^2 / 2; each horizon is the
# │          positive root of E(t) = E_max.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_linear_invalidation_horizon
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_math, fmt_magnitude, fmt_qty_int

class LatchSlotBelief:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    e0 = LatchTransformStaleness.e0  # category: illustrative (initial error at the wrist capture, calc-memory-latch-transform-staleness)
    v_drift = LatchTransformStaleness.v_drift  # category: illustrative (unobserved velocity error bound, calc-memory-latch-transform-staleness)
    a_dist = 50.0 * ureg.millimeter / ureg.second**2  # category: illustrative (disturbance acceleration bound)
    e_max = LatchTransformStaleness.e_max  # category: illustrative (latch-release slot tolerance, calc-memory-latch-transform-staleness)
    e_max_tight = 0.30 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (tighter machined slot)
    eps_sync = 0.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (clock-conversion bound, @sec-perception-observation-contract)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    def _root(e0, v, a, e_max):
        qa, qb, qc = a / 2, v, e0 - e_max
        return ((-qb + (qb**2 - 4 * qa * qc) ** 0.5) / (2 * qa)).to(millisecond)

    t_exp = _root(e0, v_drift, a_dist, e_max)
    t_exp_tight = _root(e0, v_drift, a_dist, e_max_tight)
    tol_ratio = (e_max / e_max_tight).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    horizon_ratio = (t_exp / t_exp_tight).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    t_linear = calc_linear_invalidation_horizon(e0, v_drift, e_max).to(millisecond)
    e_linear = (e0 + v_drift * t_linear + a_dist * t_linear**2 / 2).to(ureg.millimeter)
    overshoot = (e_linear / e_max - 1).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    t_extra = (t_linear - t_exp).to(millisecond)
    dt_frame = LatchTransformStaleness.dt
    e_one_frame = (e0 + v_drift * dt_frame + a_dist * dt_frame**2 / 2).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_exp.magnitude - 65.9) < 0.05, f"Latch-slot expiry should be 65.9 ms, got {t_exp}.")
    check(abs(t_exp_tight.magnitude - 16.1) < 0.05, f"Tight-slot expiry should be 16.1 ms, got {t_exp_tight}.")
    check(horizon_ratio > tol_ratio, "The horizon must shrink faster than the tolerance.")
    check(abs(t_linear.magnitude - 75.0) < 1e-9, f"Constant-velocity horizon should be 75 ms, got {t_linear}.")
    check(abs(e_linear.magnitude - 1.1406) < 1e-3, f"Bound at the constant-velocity horizon should be 1.141 mm, got {e_linear}.")
    check(t_extra.magnitude > 0, "The constant-velocity rule must admit the belief past its bounded deadline.")
    check(e_one_frame < e_max < LatchTransformStaleness.e_tool, "Consistent-epoch composition must fit the slot where the chimeric chain did not.")
    check(
        abs(eps_sync.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-9, f"Clock-conversion bound should match the perception contract's 0.2 ms, got {eps_sync}."
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    e0_str = fmt_length(e0, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    v_drift_str = fmt_velocity(v_drift, unit=ureg.millimeter / ureg.second, precision=0)
    a_dist_str = fmt_acceleration(a_dist, unit=ureg.millimeter / ureg.second**2, precision=0)
    e_max_str = fmt_length(e_max, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    e_max_tight_str = fmt_length(e_max_tight, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    t_exp_str = fmt_qty_int(t_exp, millisecond)
    t_exp_tight_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_tight, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tol_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(tol_ratio, precision=1)
    horizon_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(horizon_ratio, precision=1)
    t_linear_str = fmt_latency(t_linear, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    e_linear_str = fmt_length(e_linear, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=3)
    overshoot_str = fmt_percent(overshoot, precision=1, style="prose")
    t_extra_str = fmt_qty_int(t_extra, millisecond)
    eps_sync_str = fmt_latency(eps_sync, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    e_one_frame_str = fmt_length(e_one_frame, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)

    _e0 = fmt_magnitude(e0, ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    _v = fmt_magnitude(v_drift, ureg.millimeter / ureg.second, precision=0)
    _half_a = fmt_magnitude(a_dist / 2, ureg.millimeter / ureg.second**2, precision=0)
    _a = fmt_magnitude(a_dist, ureg.millimeter / ureg.second**2, precision=0)
    growth_math = fmt_math(rf"E(\Delta t) = {_e0} + {_v}\,\Delta t + {_half_a}\,(\Delta t)^2")
    quad_math = fmt_math(rf"{_half_a}\,(\Delta t)^2 + {_v}\,\Delta t - {fmt_magnitude(e_max - e0, ureg.millimeter, precision=1)} = 0")
    quad_tight_math = fmt_math(rf"{_half_a}\,(\Delta t)^2 + {_v}\,\Delta t - {fmt_magnitude(e_max_tight - e0, ureg.millimeter, precision=1)} = 0")
    growth_law_math = fmt_math(rf"E(t) = {_e0}\text{{ mm}} + ({_v}\text{{ mm/s}})\,t + \tfrac12({_a}\text{{ mm/s}}^2)\,t^2")
```

At the cage door, the finger now enters the slot blind. In the final approach the finger hides the slot from the wrist camera, and the finger must stay within `{python} LatchSlotBelief.e_max_str` of the slot's centerline, the task tolerance $E_{\max}$ (@fig-uncertainty-growth). For this illustrative bounded-disturbance case, suppose qualification establishes the operating region and bounds already charged at the slot's missed frame in @sec-memory-reference-frames, initial position error $E_0$ at most `{python} LatchSlotBelief.e0_str` and unobserved velocity error $v_{\text{drift}}$ at most `{python} LatchSlotBelief.v_drift_str`, and occlusion adds one more, an illustrative acceleration disturbance $a_{\text{dist}}$ at most `{python} LatchSlotBelief.a_dist_str`. The growth law of @eq-mem-occlusion-expansion carries no lever-arm arc, because the belief chains the slot against the wrist pose of its own capture epoch, the remedy for the missed frame, so position error grows only through drift and disturbance. Evaluated over the same `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.dt_str` frame period, this law gives `{python} LatchSlotBelief.e_one_frame_str` against the `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_tool_str` of the hand-composed chain; the whole difference is the lever-arm arc that consistent-epoch composition removes, which is why the same finger that failed after one missed frame now survives several.

Evaluating this growth bound with the stated parameters yields `{python} LatchSlotBelief.growth_math`, with $\Delta t$ in seconds and $E(\Delta t)$ in millimeters. Setting $E(\Delta t) = E_{\max}$ gives the quadratic equation `{python} LatchSlotBelief.quad_math`. Its single positive real root is `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_exp_str`, so dependent motion must cease relying on this belief by then, with any necessary response initiated earlier. If the slot were machined to a clearance of `{python} LatchSlotBelief.e_max_tight_str`, the allowable unobserved duration shrinks to `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_exp_tight_str` (`{python} LatchSlotBelief.quad_tight_math`). Tightening mechanical tolerance by `{python} LatchSlotBelief.tol_ratio_mult_str` shrinks the allowable unobserved duration by `{python} LatchSlotBelief.horizon_ratio_mult_str`, requiring sensor re-acquisition or compliant impedance holding within that shorter window. In contrast, if an estimator naively assumes constant velocity ($a_{\text{dist}} = 0$), it predicts a valid horizon of $(E_{\max} - E_0)/v_{\text{drift}}$, or `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_linear_str`. At that elapsed time the modeled bound reaches `{python} LatchSlotBelief.e_linear_str`, exceeding the clearance by `{python} LatchSlotBelief.overshoot_str`. A constant-velocity-only admission rule would keep accepting the estimate for `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_extra_str` beyond the bounded-model deadline; whether contact occurs depends on the path and geometry.

::: {#fig-uncertainty-growth fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Belief uncertainty and invalidation horizon**: Illustrative spatial error bound $E(\\Delta t)$ of a gripper finger entering the cage door's latch-release slot, expanding quadratically under unobserved forward propagation until intersecting the slot clearance $E_{\\max} = 1\\text{ mm}$ at invalidation horizon $T_{\\text{inv}} = 66\\text{ ms}$. A dashed constant-velocity estimate grows more slowly, and the red marker shows that estimate still admitting the belief after the bounded error has passed the clearance. Belief has a shelf life governed by physical disturbance dynamics, and only qualified new evidence can renew the relevant state claim." fig-alt="Belief uncertainty growth and invalidation horizon plot. Spatial error bound E(Δt) plotted against elapsed time Δt since last measurement. The quadratic curve expands from E0 = 0.1 mm to intersect task clearance E_max = 1 mm at invalidation horizon T_inv = 66 ms. A dashed constant-velocity line rises more slowly, and a red marker on the bounded curve shows the belief that estimate still admits after the curve has crossed the clearance."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BELIEF UNCERTAINTY AND INVALIDATION HORIZON (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-uncertainty-growth
# │ Goal:    show that a belief has a shelf life set by disturbance dynamics
# │ Show:    the bounded error growth against task clearance, and what a
# │          constant-velocity estimator would have admitted instead
# │ How:     E(dt) = e0 + v*dt + a*dt^2; the horizon is its positive root
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
E0 = LatchSlotBelief.e0.to(
    ureg.millimeter
).magnitude  # mm, residual error at the last observation  # category: illustrative (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion cell)
V_DIST = LatchSlotBelief.v_drift.to(
    ureg.millimeter / ureg.second
).magnitude  # mm/s, bounded disturbance velocity  # category: illustrative (as above)
A_DIST = (
    (LatchSlotBelief.a_dist / 2).to(ureg.millimeter / ureg.second**2).magnitude
)  # mm/s^2, half the bounded disturbance acceleration (a_dist / 2)  # category: illustrative (as above)
E_MAX = LatchSlotBelief.e_max.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude  # mm, task clearance  # category: illustrative (as above)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
bounded = lambda dt: E0 + V_DIST * dt + A_DIST * dt**2
linear = lambda dt: E0 + V_DIST * dt

# positive root of A dt^2 + V dt + (E0 - E_MAX) = 0
t_exp = (-V_DIST + np.sqrt(V_DIST**2 - 4 * A_DIST * (E0 - E_MAX))) / (2 * A_DIST)
t_linear = (E_MAX - E0) / V_DIST  # what constant velocity predicts
overshoot = bounded(t_linear) / E_MAX - 1.0  # by how much that overruns

dt = np.linspace(0, 0.120, 400)

# ┌── 3. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.plot(dt * 1000, bounded(dt), color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=2.4, label="bounded growth  $E(\\Delta t)$", zorder=4)
ax.plot(dt * 1000, linear(dt), color=COLORS["primary"], lw=1.6, ls=(0, (6, 3)), label="constant-velocity estimate", zorder=3)
ax.axhline(E_MAX, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.4, ls=(0, (5, 4)), zorder=3)
ax.text(2, E_MAX * 1.03, f"task clearance $E_{{\\max}}$ = {E_MAX:.0f} mm", color=COLORS["RedLine"], fontsize=9, va="bottom")

ax.plot([t_exp * 1000], [E_MAX], "o", ms=7, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], zorder=6)
ax.vlines(t_exp * 1000, 0, E_MAX, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1, 2)), zorder=3)
ax.annotate(
    f"invalidation horizon\n$T_{{inv}}$ = {t_exp*1000:.0f} ms",
    xy=(t_exp * 1000, E_MAX),
    xytext=(t_exp * 1000 - 8, E_MAX * 1.55),
    fontsize=9,
    color=COLORS["BlueLine"],
    ha="right",
    zorder=6,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=0.9),
)

ax.plot([t_linear * 1000], [bounded(t_linear)], "o", ms=7, color=COLORS["RedLine"], zorder=6)
ax.annotate(
    f"still admitted at {t_linear*1000:.0f} ms:\n" f"{bounded(t_linear):.3f} mm, {overshoot*100:.1f}% over clearance",
    xy=(t_linear * 1000, bounded(t_linear)),
    xytext=(84, 0.52),
    fontsize=8.5,
    color=COLORS["RedLine"],
    ha="left",
    zorder=6,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=0.9),
)

ax.set_xlim(0, 120)
ax.set_ylim(0, 2.1)
ax.set_xlabel("Elapsed time since last observation, $\\Delta t$ (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("Spatial error bound, $E(\\Delta t)$ (mm)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The preceding examples bound position error directly. An estimator's internal **covariance matrix**\index{Covariance matrix} instead describes the spread of a stochastic error model, not a measured hard maximum. Its entries have squared physical units, so variance growth cannot be substituted directly for the distance bound used in the expiry calculation. To see why stochastic uncertainty disperses so aggressively during sensor dropout, consider a kinematic body whose continuous-time translational acceleration is subject to unmodeled disturbance or actuator jitter modeled as zero-mean continuous Gaussian white noise: $\ddot{\mathbf{p}}(t) = \mathbf{w}(t)$, with $\mathbf{w}(t) \sim \mathcal{WN}(0, \mathbf{Q}_c)$, where $\mathbf{Q}_c = q_c \mathbf{I}$ represents the continuous power spectral density of acceleration noise with physical units $\text{m}^2/\text{s}^3$.

Integrating acceleration once yields velocity $\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{v}(0) + \int_0^t \mathbf{w}(\tau)\,d\tau$. Integrating a second time over elapsed duration $t$ gives the physical position:
$$\mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{p}(0) + \mathbf{v}(0)t + \int_0^t (t-\tau)\mathbf{w}(\tau)\,d\tau$$

To isolate the process-noise contribution, assume the initial position and velocity are known exactly. During an occlusion gap where external measurement updates drop out, an estimator propagates state forward using its nominal transition model $\hat{\mathbf{p}}(t) = \hat{\mathbf{p}}(0) + \hat{\mathbf{v}}(0)t$. The unobserved position error covariance $\mathbf{P}_{pp}(t) = \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{p}(t) - \hat{\mathbf{p}}(t))(\mathbf{p}(t) - \hat{\mathbf{p}}(t))^T]$ accumulates the continuous noise variance across the double integration:
$$\mathbf{P}_{pp}(t) = \int_0^t (t-\tau)^2 q_c \mathbf{I}\,d\tau = q_c \mathbf{I} \left[ -\frac{(t-\tau)^3}{3} \right]_0^t = \frac{1}{3} q_c t^3 \mathbf{I}$$

Double integration makes this process-noise contribution grow cubically with elapsed time. With nonzero initial uncertainty, the total covariance must also include the propagated initial position and velocity covariance and their cross-covariance; the integral above is only the additional process term. That result explains why extrapolation needs a widening error model even when its predicted trajectory remains smooth. It does not turn covariance into a physical distance bound. A consumer first converts the variance to a margin using a justified coverage level, then combines that margin with bias and other errors omitted by the stochastic model. The nominal hull can, for example, be inflated to $r_{\text{inflated}}(t) = r_{\text{hull}} + k \sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{P}_{pp}(t))}$ when that coverage construction has been calibrated. The permission mechanism that uses the resulting clearance is developed in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission; the memory contract must supply the bound and its assumptions before that mechanism can help.

A safety argument can rest on one of two kinds of bound. A **bounded-disturbance** growth law needs justified limits on initial error, velocity, acceleration, clock conversion, and mode changes; then the `{python} RackEndBelief.t_exp_ahead_str` aisle-ahead root and the `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_exp_str` latch-slot root are conditional worst-case deadlines within that region. Alternatively, staged dropouts and external ground truth can calibrate a specified residual quantile (for example $P_{99}$ or $P_{99.9}$) under a named test distribution. That yields a probabilistic admission limit with a 1 percent or 0.1 percent tail before other model and coverage errors. The record and consumer must declare which regime applies, monitor its validity region, and refuse dependent motion or choose a validated feasible fallback when evidence exceeds it.

Either regime yields the same kind of deadline, because the invalidation horizon of \ref{dfn-memory-belief-invalidation-horizon} asks only when the declared bound first reaches the task tolerance, whatever model produced the bound. Expiry is therefore neither an arbitrary communication watchdog timer nor a fixed $100\text{ ms}$ heuristic chosen for scheduling convenience. It is a physical deadline dictated by task geometry, actuator authority, and disturbance dynamics, and past $t_0 + T_{\text{inv}}$ no downstream loop may assume the estimated pose lies within the required clearance.

The horizon of @eq-mem-invalidation-horizon is not one scalar for the whole machine. Payload, speed, and contact state change the disturbance bounds, so the state interface selects the active expiry for the current operating regime, and a transition from free motion into contact, which changes velocity within milliseconds, invalidates a smooth drift model outright. Beliefs on the same machine expire on different clocks (@tbl-09-belief-decay-horizons). The latch-slot finger is bounded by drift and disturbance acting against a millimeter tolerance. The free space around the base and a coworker beside the arm are all bounded by the same walking speed, yet those beliefs lapse at different times because each starts from a different initial error and closes on a different tolerance; for free space, the tolerance is the depth to the nearest unobserved boundary.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-expiry-roots
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BELIEF-EXPIRY ROOTS ON THE MACHINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-09-belief-decay-horizons (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion).
# │
# │ Goal:    Set the machine's beliefs side by side: free space abreast of the
# │          rack end and in the aisle ahead, a coworker beside the arm, and
# │          the latch-slot finger.
# │ Show:    each row's growth law and its root against the task limit.
# │ How:     E(t) = E0 + v t + a t^2 / 2; the root is the positive solution of
# │          E(t) = E_max. The coworker and free-space rows are bounded by
# │          the ISO walking speed, so a = 0 and E(t) is linear; free-space
# │          limits are d_free - delta_margin. The rack-end and latch-slot rows
# │          reuse the chapter's RackEndBelief and LatchSlotBelief cells.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_math, fmt_magnitude, fmt_qty_int

class MachineExpiryRoots:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    cw_e0 = 15.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (coworker position error at last observation)
    cw_v = RackEndBelief.v_h.to(ureg.millimeter / ureg.second)  # category: datasheet (ISO 13855 walking speed, calc-memory-rack-end)
    cw_e_max = 150.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: chosen (belief tolerance to the arm's swept volume; not the planner's obstacle clearance)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    cw_t_exp = ((cw_e_max - cw_e0) / cw_v).to(millisecond)  # v_h bounds speed directly, so a_dist = 0

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(cw_t_exp.magnitude - 84.375) < 1e-9, f"Coworker expiry should be 84.375 ms, got {cw_t_exp}.")
    check(
        RackEndBelief.t_exp_abreast < LatchSlotBelief.t_exp < cw_t_exp < RackEndBelief.t_exp_ahead,
        "Rows must order rack end, latch-slot finger, coworker, aisle ahead.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    _mm, _mms = ureg.millimeter, ureg.millimeter / ureg.second
    rack_growth_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt_magnitude(RackEndBelief.delta_loc, _mm, precision=0)}+{fmt_magnitude(RackEndBelief.v_h, _mms, precision=0)}t")
    rack_limit_str = fmt_magnitude(RackEndBelief.side_clearance - RackEndBelief.delta_margin, _mm, precision=0)
    rack_root_str = RackEndBelief.t_exp_abreast_str
    ahead_limit_str = fmt_magnitude(RackEndBelief.d_clear - RackEndBelief.delta_margin, _mm, precision=0)
    ahead_root_str = RackEndBelief.t_exp_ahead_str
    cw_growth_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt_magnitude(cw_e0, _mm, precision=0)}+{fmt_magnitude(cw_v, _mms, precision=0)}t")
    cw_limit_str = fmt_magnitude(cw_e_max, _mm, precision=0)
    cw_root_str = fmt_qty_int(cw_t_exp, millisecond)
    latch_growth_math = fmt_math(rf"{LatchSlotBelief._e0}+{LatchSlotBelief._v}t+{LatchSlotBelief._half_a}t^2")
    latch_limit_str = fmt_magnitude(LatchSlotBelief.e_max, _mm, precision=0)
    latch_root_str = LatchSlotBelief.t_exp_str
```

| Belief                             | Error bound $E(t)$ (mm; $t$ in s)               |                               Task limit (mm) |                                         Root | Response at expiry                                                  |
|:-----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------------:|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Free space abreast of the rack end | `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.rack_growth_math`  |  `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.rack_limit_str` |  `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.rack_root_str` | Treat the cross aisle as unknown; refuse dependent advance          |
| Free space to the rack end ahead   | `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.rack_growth_math`  | `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.ahead_limit_str` | `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.ahead_root_str` | Refuse motion that relies on the claim; renew from the next frame   |
| Latch-slot finger                  | `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.latch_growth_math` | `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.latch_limit_str` | `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.latch_root_str` | Refuse the insertion; hold compliantly or reacquire the slot        |
| Coworker beside the arm            | `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.cw_growth_math`    |    `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.cw_limit_str` |    `{python} MachineExpiryRoots.cw_root_str` | Revoke dependent arm motion; stop only if braking clearance remains |

: **Belief-expiry roots on the machine**: Each root solves $E(t)=E_{\max}$ for that belief's error model and task limit. The two free-space rows are @eq-mem-free-space-expiry, with limits set by the depth to the nearest unobserved boundary less the protective clearance. The coworker's initial error is illustrative and its tolerance chosen, while its speed is the same walking-speed bound, so all three person rows grow linearly. The last column names the required disposition by that root; any physical response must begin early enough to remain feasible. The record for the mug-handle belief that @sec-intent consumes is filled in @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema. {#tbl-09-belief-decay-horizons tbl-colwidths="[20,28,14,12,26]"}

Every root in this section trusts the growth law it was computed from. A growth law is only as good as the machine's ability to catch its failures, through a residual at reacquisition or a staged dropout test, and some errors produce no residual at all because no sensor on the machine can see them.

## Observability Ceilings and Estimation Limits {#sec-memory-state-estimation-bounds}

A force sensor can report the same value when contact force rises as when its electronic offset drifts. Repeated samples of that value do not by themselves distinguish the two causes. The problem is observability: whether the available measurements and known dynamics can distinguish the physical states the controller needs. The instantaneous measurement model illustrates the issue. An observation mapping $\mathbf{y} = h(\mathbf{x})$ can map distinct physical states $\mathbf{x}_1 \neq \mathbf{x}_2$ to the same reading ($h(\mathbf{x}_1) = h(\mathbf{x}_2)$). In the force-plus-bias example, compensating changes in force and bias form a locally insensitive direction in the observation Jacobian $\mathbf{H} = \partial h / \partial \mathbf{x}$. That direction lies in the Jacobian's null space, the set of state changes that produce no local change in the reading. The measurement likelihood has zero sensitivity along that direction; in the special case where the entire state is unconstrained, $\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}$. Instantaneous ambiguity alone does not establish unobservability over time; motion can make the states distinguishable in later measurements. If the ambiguity persists along the operating trajectory, processing the same measurements cannot resolve it. Parameter scaling increases representational capacity, but it cannot synthesize physical information that never crossed the causal boundary.

Observability depends on the available measurements and operating trajectory. When a disturbance changes the needed state without changing those measurements, an estimator can enter the **zero-innovation trap**\index{Zero-innovation trap!definition}. The residual vanishes ($\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{0}$), yet a filter whose model omits the hidden drift may report contracting covariance. Repeated agreement with the same sensor then strengthens a mistaken estimate without supplying the missing physical constraint.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-bias-drift
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ILLUSTRATIVE STRAIN-GAUGE BIAS DRIFT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-state-estimation-bounds (unobservable sensor bias).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show a confident estimate drifting along an unobservable subspace.
# │ Show:    5 N reading; 0.2 N/min thermal drift over 15 min shifts the bias
# │          by 3 N, so the true force is 2 N, 60 percent below nominal.
# │ How:     Illustrative reading, drift rate, and span; shift = rate x span.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_force, fmt_int, check

class MemoryBiasDrift:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    y_read = 5.0 * newton  # category: illustrative (steady strain-gauge reading)
    sigma_claim = 0.05 * newton  # category: illustrative (estimator's reported P99 bound)
    drift_rate = 0.2 * newton / minute  # category: illustrative (thermoelastic bias drift)
    span = 15 * minute  # category: illustrative (drift interval)
    t_excite = 40 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (deliberate contact break)
    f_sample = 1000 * hertz  # category: illustrative (strain-gauge sample rate)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    shift = (drift_rate * span).to(newton)
    x_true = (y_read - shift).to(newton)
    pct = (shift / y_read).to("dimensionless").magnitude * 100

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(shift.magnitude - 3.0) < 1e-9, "Bias shift is 3 N.")
    check(abs(x_true.magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "True force falls to 2 N.")
    check(abs(pct - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Drift is 60 percent of nominal.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    y_str = fmt_force(y_read, precision=0)
    zero_str = fmt_force(0 * newton, precision=0)
    sigma_str = fmt_force(sigma_claim, precision=2)
    rate_str = fmt(drift_rate.magnitude, precision=1)
    span_str = fmt_int(span.magnitude)
    shift_str = fmt_force(shift, precision=0)
    x_true_str = fmt_force(x_true, precision=0)
    pct_str = fmt_int(pct)
    t_excite_str = fmt_int(t_excite.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    f_sample_str = fmt_int(f_sample.to(hertz).magnitude)
```

An illustrative strain gauge on a robot's end-effector reads a steady `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.y_str`, a reading that fits any true contact force once an unknown bias is allowed. An estimator, or a learned model, that predicts that force with confidence has not shown the force is observable. In state estimation, a state trajectory is **observable**\index{Observable} if and only if the history of available sensor outputs over a finite time window uniquely determines the initial state of the machine, so that distinct physical trajectories produce distinct sensor trajectories rather than indistinguishable measurement sequences. When two distinct physical state histories produce the exact same sequence of sensor readings, no mathematical operation, filter, or neural network running anywhere in the machine can determine which physical trajectory the body actually followed. The machine receives identical bitstreams from its sensor interfaces across both realities.

To see why predictability differs from observability, follow that end-effector as it regulates contact force against a rigid surface. Let the true normal contact force be $x(t)$, and let the strain-gauge conditioning electronics introduce an unknown, slowly changing sensor bias $b(t)$. The raw measurement delivered to the estimator at each sample interval is $y(t) = x(t) + b(t)$. Suppose the sensor outputs a constant stream $y(t) =$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.y_str`. This observation is satisfied by a true physical force $x(t) =$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.y_str` with zero offset $b(t) =$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.zero_str`. It is equally satisfied by a true force $x(t) =$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.x_true_str` with a sensor bias $b(t) =$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.shift_str`, or by $x(t) =$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.zero_str` with a bias $b(t) =$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.y_str`. For any arbitrary offset trajectory $\Delta(t)$, the state pair $(x(t) - \Delta(t), b(t) + \Delta(t))$ produces the exact same measurement sequence $y(t)$. The difference between the true force and the sensor offset lies in an **unobservable subspace**\index{Unobservable subspace} of the measurement system, a structural blind spot where physical variations perfectly cancel each other out in the sensor data.

Because the measurement stream cannot distinguish between physical load and sensor drift, an estimator must rely on prior assumptions about how each state evolves. If a Kalman filter or a learned recurrent estimator is configured with a belief that the sensor offset $b(t)$ is static with near-zero variance, it attributes every variation in $y(t)$ to changes in true contact force $x(t)$. As new samples arrive at `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.f_sample_str` $\text{Hz}$, the filter incorporates the incoming data, repeatedly updating its internal state. Because the incoming measurements match the forward projection of the state dynamics, the calculated state covariance contracts, and the estimator reports an increasingly narrow uncertainty bound, publishing an estimate of `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.y_str` $\pm$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.sigma_str` at $P_{99}$. Meanwhile, thermal dissipation from nearby joint actuators warms the end-effector structure, causing the sensor bias $b(t)$ to drift at `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.rate_str` $\text{N/min}$. Over `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.span_str` $\text{min}$, $b(t)$ shifts by `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.shift_str`. The true force on the surface has fallen from `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.y_str` to `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.x_true_str`, yet the estimator reports high confidence in a state that has drifted by `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.pct_str` percent of its nominal value.

The downstream control policy responds to this false certainty by commanding motor torques to maintain what it believes is a `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.y_str` preload. If the workpiece needs more frictional support than that reduced preload supplies, it can slip even while the reported force remains on target. The force estimate alone cannot reveal the loss of support. The estimator monitors its innovation sequence\index{Innovation sequence}, the innovation of @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion evaluated at every sample between incoming measurements $y(t)$ and predicted measurements $\hat{y}(t)$. In this drift scenario, the estimator predicted $\hat{y}(t) = \hat{x}(t) + \hat{b}(t) =$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.y_str`, and the physical sensor returned $y(t) =$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.y_str`. The innovation is zero at every time step. An innovation check measures only whether the physical sensors disagree with the forward projection of the internal state. It cannot expose an unobservable error mode, because along the unobservable manifold the sensor output is invariant to the drift.

Recovering observability requires the system architecture to provide an additional constraint that breaks the symmetry along the unobservable subspace. An engineering design accomplishes this in one of three ways. First, independent sensing can introduce a second measurement channel with different failure physics, such as monitoring joint motor current or an optical deflection sensor that does not share the strain gauge's thermal sensitivity. Second, the machine can perform deliberate physical excitation, after independently supporting the workpiece, commanding the gripper to briefly break contact for `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.t_excite_str` $\text{ms}$, creating a known boundary condition of $x(t) =$ `{python} MemoryBiasDrift.zero_str` where the measured sensor value directly exposes $b(t)$. Third, the machine can rely on periodic external anchoring, bringing the tool into contact with a calibrated reference load cell during scheduled tool-change cycles to reset the bias estimate.

When a physical state cannot be constrained by complementary sensing or active excitation, the estimator must treat that state as unobservable and refuse to publish false precision. The estimation layer must mark the corresponding state dimensions as unavailable, or widen their error bound according to the worst-case physical drift rate of the underlying hardware rather than the contracted covariance of a filtering algorithm. Formal observability analysis for linear and nonlinear dynamic systems is an established foundation of control theory, treated rigorously by @kalman1960general for linear state spaces and by @hermann1977nonlinear for nonlinear systems via differential observability rank conditions (see @sec-appendix-control-covariance). A systems engineer does not rederive these rank conditions at runtime. The engineering task is to identify which physical states lack full observability rank under the current sensor suite, and to enforce that the state interface never reports statistical convergence on an unconstrained degree of freedom.

Deterministic observability concerns whether the stated dynamics and sensor model distinguish states along the operating trajectory; it does not depend on a zero-mean noise assumption. Estimator convergence and the coverage of its reported uncertainty require additional, model-specific conditions. These can include calibrated physical parameters, adequate excitation, and justified assumptions about noise means and correlations. A trajectory that enters a singular configuration may also lose observability rank. Runtime checks therefore monitor the conditions the particular estimate requires, using redundant channels, environmental measurements, and qualified re-zeroing routines. These checks cannot prove every modeling assumption, but a detected violation must withdraw the dependent estimate's valid status. Downstream controllers then use a validated feasible fallback. An estimator that withdraws its own claim fails in the open; the harder failures are the ones in which nothing withdraws.

## Spatial Belief Failure Modes and Map Corruption {#sec-memory-failure-modes}

The fundamental failure modes of spatial memory rarely announce themselves with operating system exceptions or kernel panic logs. A corrupted pointer or a segmentation fault can expose a process failure, although a separate fallback path must still bring motion under control. In contrast, spatial memory failures are predominantly silent and deceptive: the memory subsystem continues publishing well-formed, syntactically valid data structures at high frequency, while the geometric coordinates inside those structures have parted ways with physical reality.

This divergence exposes the **middleware QoS mirage**\index{Middleware QoS mirage!definition}. Modern robotics middlewares and distributed messaging fabrics (such as ROS 2, DDS, or gRPC streaming) provide Quality of Service (QoS) policies like `Deadline` and `Liveliness`. However, these policies monitor only network sockets and thread execution heartbeats; they confirm that a publisher process is running and sending packets at the nominal cadence. If an upstream camera driver deadlocks or an object tracker drops tracking while republishing its last cached matrix, DDS reports 100 percent QoS health. Middleware cannot inspect the physical validity of its payload, allowing dangerous frozen transforms, stale state-store entries, and phantom tracks to pass directly to motor controllers.

```{python}
#| label: calc-memory-frozen-transform
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ILLUSTRATIVE FROZEN-TRANSFORM TIMELINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-memory-failure-modes (loud and silent failures, frozen
# │          transform).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show a republished stale transform passing a publish-time check
# │          while tracking error grows.
# │ Show:    1 ms republish period (1000 Hz); 5 ms freshness threshold; sensor
# │          lost at 10 ms; 0.5 m/s object motion gives 50 mm in 100 ms.
# │ How:     Illustrative timeline; error = speed x elapsed time.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, check

class MemoryFrozenTransform:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    t_repub = 1 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (middleware republish period)
    tau_max = 5 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (publish-time freshness threshold)
    t_loss = 10 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (sensor stops producing evidence)
    v_obj = 0.5 * meter / second  # category: illustrative (object speed)
    t_window = 100 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (elapsed time with static transform)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    f_repub = (1 / t_repub).to(hertz)
    err = (v_obj * t_window).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t_repub < tau_max, "A republished copy must pass the freshness threshold.")
    check(abs(err.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tracking error is 50 mm.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_repub_str = fmt_int(t_repub.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    tau_max_str = fmt_int(tau_max.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    t_loss_str = fmt_int(t_loss.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    f_repub_str = fmt_int(f_repub.magnitude)
    v_obj_str = fmt(v_obj.magnitude, precision=1)
    t_window_str = fmt_int(t_window.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    err_str = fmt_int(err.magnitude)
```

A camera stops delivering frames, yet a transport node keeps republishing its last transform with the current time, and a downstream controller's `{python} MemoryFrozenTransform.tau_max_str` $\text{ms}$ publish-time freshness check passes every copy. That failure differs in kind from a camera that simply falls silent, and the difference sorts every estimation failure into one of two forms. In a **loud failure**\index{Loud failure}, a component halts execution, drops a communication packet, clears an output buffer, or asserts an explicit error bit. Downstream consumers immediately observe the absence of data or the cleared validity flag, enabling a validated fallback, such as a hold, stop, or compliant mode, when one remains feasible. In a **silent failure**\index{Silent failure}, the memory layer continues to publish a complete, numerically well-formed state record with valid status bits, low variance indicators, and continuous timestamps, while the numbers inside the record diverge from the physical configuration of the machine. Downstream control loops consume these corrupted records without raising an exception, computing feedback corrections against a phantom geometry. Because physical actuators execute commands derived from these valid-looking records, such as driving an arm toward a target that now intersects a wall, silent state corruption can deliver force across the causal boundary of @sec-boundary-causal-boundary before any software monitor registers an anomaly.[^fn-std-amr-occlusion]

[^fn-std-amr-occlusion]: **AMR Safety Standards**\index{AMR Safety Standards}: ISO 3691-4:2023 [@iso3691part4] addresses safety requirements for driverless industrial trucks and their systems. Occlusion and stopping distance are assessed for each design's operating domain and sensor and actuator configuration, not taken as universal values.

The republishing hazard of @sec-memory-preserving-belief has a name, the **frozen transform**\index{Frozen transform}, and it is the most deceptive silent failure because a stale spatial snapshot, republished with current timestamps, masks a dead sensor. In an illustrative timeline, an optical tracking node computes a transformation matrix $T_{\text{camera}}^{\text{object}}$ at timestamp $t_0 = 0\text{ ms}$. If the optical sensor disconnects, drops frames, or suffers thread starvation at $t =$ `{python} MemoryFrozenTransform.t_loss_str` $\text{ms}$, the underlying tracking algorithm ceases to produce new spatial evidence. If the message-passing middleware or an intermediate transport node retains the last computed matrix in an unexpired buffer and republishes it at a loop rate of `{python} MemoryFrozenTransform.f_repub_str` $\text{Hz}$, generating a new transmission timestamp $t_k = t_0 + k\,T_{\text{rep}}$ with $T_{\text{rep}} =$ `{python} MemoryFrozenTransform.t_repub_str` $\text{ms}$, the temporal provenance of the measurement is erased. A downstream tracking controller verifies freshness by computing data age as $\Delta t = t_{\text{now}} - t_{\text{msg}}$.
